Week 15 · Phase 4: Advanced Topics

Deep Reinforcement Learning

Learning to act from reward. MDPs, returns, value functions and the Bellman equations (derived), dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning (Q-learning, SARSA), function approximation and the deadly triad, DQN with replay and target networks, Double, Dueling and prioritized variants, the policy gradient theorem (derived), REINFORCE with baselines, actor-critic, GAE (derived), A2C/A3C, TRPO and PPO, continuous control (DDPG, TD3, SAC), exploration, model-based RL and world models, offline RL, and the connection to language models (RLHF, reward models, PPO, DPO, GRPO). The lab trains DQN on CartPole in PyTorch and PPO with Stable-Baselines3.

95 min read4 interactive demos12 figures15 code blocks11 exercises
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • Formalize a sequential decision problem as a Markov decision process and define return, policy, state-value and action-value functions.
  • Derive the Bellman expectation and optimality equations and use them for policy evaluation, policy iteration and value iteration.
  • Contrast Monte Carlo and temporal-difference estimates in terms of bias and variance, and explain why Q-learning is off-policy while SARSA is on-policy.
  • Explain the deadly triad (function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy data) and how DQN's replay buffer and target network mitigate it.
  • Describe Double DQN, Dueling DQN and prioritized experience replay and the specific failure each one repairs.
  • Derive the policy gradient theorem, REINFORCE, the baseline trick and generalized advantage estimation (GAE), and explain the bias-variance role of λ\lambdaλ.
  • Explain A2C/A3C, TRPO's trust region, and PPO's clipped objective, and predict how the clip changes the gradient.
  • Compare DDPG, TD3 and SAC for continuous control and write the maximum-entropy objective.
  • Summarize exploration strategies, model-based RL and world models, and offline RL with its distribution-shift problem.
  • Describe the RLHF pipeline (supervised fine-tuning, reward model, PPO with a KL penalty) and how DPO and GRPO relate to it.
  • Implement DQN from scratch in PyTorch for CartPole and train PPO with Stable-Baselines3.

Everything in the previous weeks learned from a fixed dataset of labelled examples or from raw data. Reinforcement learning (RL) changes the problem. There is no teacher that says what the right output is. An agent takes actions in a world, the world responds with a new situation and a scalar reward, and the agent must discover, by trial and error, how to act so that the total reward over time is large. A chess program learns from a single win or loss at the end of a game that may have lasted eighty moves; a robot learns to walk from a signal that says only how far it travelled; a language model is tuned toward answers that human raters prefer. Three difficulties distinguish this from supervised learning: credit assignment (which of the many past actions deserves credit for the reward?), exploration (the agent only sees the consequences of what it tries, so it must choose what to try), and non-stationarity (the data the agent trains on depends on the agent's own current behaviour, so the data distribution moves as it learns).

Deep RL is RL in which the policy, the value function, or a model of the world is a neural network. It produced the best-known demonstrations of the last decade: DQN playing Atari from pixels (2013-2015), AlphaGo and AlphaZero (2016-2017), OpenAI Five and AlphaStar, dexterous robot hands, plasma control in tokamaks, and, most relevant to this course, the post-training of large language models with human feedback. It is also notoriously fragile: results depend on seeds, hyper-parameters and implementation details far more than in supervised learning. This week gives you the theory you need to know why the algorithms look the way they do, and the practice to run them and diagnose them.

The structure follows the logic of the field. We first fix the formalism (MDPs, value functions, Bellman equations). We then build the tabular toolbox (dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, temporal-difference learning), because every deep algorithm is one of these ideas with a network inside. Value-based deep RL (DQN and its repairs) comes next, then policy-gradient methods (REINFORCE, actor-critic, GAE, PPO), then continuous control, exploration, model-based and offline RL, and finally how all of this is used on language models. Notation follows Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed., 2018), the standard text.

Markov decision processes

The standard model of a sequential decision problem is the Markov decision process (MDP), a tuple (S,A,p,r,γ)(\mathcal S,\mathcal A,p,r,\gamma)(S,A,p,r,γ):

  • S\mathcal SS is the set of states and A\mathcal AA the set of actions (both can be finite, as in a board game, or continuous, as in joint torques).
  • p(s′∣s,a)p(s'\mid s,a)p(s′∣s,a) is the transition probability: the chance that taking action aaa in state sss leads to state s′s's′.
  • r(s,a)r(s,a)r(s,a) (or r(s,a,s′)r(s,a,s')r(s,a,s′)) is the reward function; Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​ denotes the random reward received after the action at time ttt.
  • γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1]γ∈[0,1] is the discount factor, explained below.

The defining assumption is the Markov property: the next state and reward depend on the history only through the current state and action, Pr⁡(St+1,Rt+1∣S0,A0,…,St,At)=Pr⁡(St+1,Rt+1∣St,At)\Pr(S_{t+1},R_{t+1}\mid S_0,A_0,\dots,S_t,A_t)=\Pr(S_{t+1},R_{t+1}\mid S_t,A_t)Pr(St+1​,Rt+1​∣S0​,A0​,…,St​,At​)=Pr(St+1​,Rt+1​∣St​,At​). The state is a sufficient statistic of the past. This is a statement about how you define the state: if a single Atari frame does not reveal the velocity of the ball, it is not Markov, but a stack of four frames nearly is, and that is exactly why DQN feeds four frames to its network. When the observation is not Markov, the problem is a partially observable MDP (POMDP), and the agent needs memory (recurrent networks or attention over history, as in Week 7 and Week 9).

A policy π(a∣s)\pi(a\mid s)π(a∣s) is the agent's rule for acting: a distribution over actions for each state (a deterministic policy is the special case with all mass on one action, written a=μ(s)a=\mu(s)a=μ(s)). Following π\piπ from a start state generates a trajectory τ=(S0,A0,R1,S1,A1,R2,… )\tau=(S_0,A_0,R_1,S_1,A_1,R_2,\dots)τ=(S0​,A0​,R1​,S1​,A1​,R2​,…). The goal is to find the policy that maximizes the expected sum of rewards.

Returns and discounting

The return from time ttt is the discounted sum of future rewards:

Gt  =  Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+⋯  =  ∑k=0∞γkRt+k+1.G_t \;=\; R_{t+1}+\gamma R_{t+2}+\gamma^2 R_{t+3}+\cdots \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{k}R_{t+k+1}.Gt​=Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+⋯=k=0∑∞​γkRt+k+1​.

A reward kkk steps in the future is worth γk\gamma^kγk of an immediate one. Discounting does three jobs. It keeps the sum finite for infinitely long tasks when rewards are bounded (∣Gt∣≤Rmax⁡/(1−γ)|G_t|\le R_{\max}/(1-\gamma)∣Gt​∣≤Rmax​/(1−γ)). It encodes a preference for sooner rewards, and it reduces variance, because distant rewards, which are the most uncertain, count for less. Its effective horizon is about 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma)1/(1−γ) steps: with γ=0.99\gamma=0.99γ=0.99 the agent looks around 100 steps ahead, with γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9 about ten. Choosing γ\gammaγ is therefore a modelling decision about how far ahead the agent should plan, not just a numerical convenience. A useful recursion follows directly from the definition and is the seed of everything below:

Gt=Rt+1+γGt+1.G_t = R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}.Gt​=Rt+1​+γGt+1​.

Many tasks are episodic: they end in a terminal state (a game is won, a pole falls over), after which the environment resets. Episodic tasks can use γ=1\gamma=1γ=1; in that case the sum is finite because the episode is. At a terminal state we define the value of the next state to be zero, which in code becomes the (1 - done) mask that you will see in every implementation.

Value functions

Rewards are immediate; what the agent needs is a way to judge how good it is to be somewhere. The state-value function of a policy is the expected return when starting in sss and following π\piπ thereafter, and the action-value function (or Q-function) is the expected return when starting in sss, taking action aaa first, and following π\piπ afterwards:

vπ(s)=Eπ ⁣[Gt∣St=s],qπ(s,a)=Eπ ⁣[Gt∣St=s,At=a].v_\pi(s)=\E_\pi\!\left[G_t\mid S_t=s\right],\qquad q_\pi(s,a)=\E_\pi\!\left[G_t\mid S_t=s,A_t=a\right].vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s],qπ​(s,a)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s,At​=a].

The two are linked by averaging over the policy: vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s) qπ(s,a)v_\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\,q_\pi(s,a)vπ​(s)=∑a​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a). The difference Aπ(s,a)=qπ(s,a)−vπ(s)A_\pi(s,a)=q_\pi(s,a)-v_\pi(s)Aπ​(s,a)=qπ​(s,a)−vπ​(s) is the advantage: how much better action aaa is than the policy's average behaviour in sss. Advantages will be the central quantity of policy-gradient methods. Note what a value function is: a prediction of future reward under a particular behaviour, learnt from experience. It turns the hard, delayed credit-assignment problem into a local one: if you have a good vvv, you can judge an action immediately by the value of where it leads.

The Bellman equations

The recursion Gt=Rt+1+γGt+1G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}Gt​=Rt+1​+γGt+1​ gives a self-consistency condition on value functions. Deriving it is short and worth doing carefully, since every algorithm this week is an attempt to enforce, approximate or exploit it.

Derivation: Bellman expectation equation

Start from the definition and substitute the return recursion: vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣St=s]=Eπ[Rt+1+γGt+1∣St=s]=∑aπ(a∣s)∑s′p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γ Eπ[Gt+1∣St+1=s′]]=∑aπ(a∣s)∑s′p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γ vπ(s′)].\begin{aligned} v_\pi(s) &= \E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s] \\ &= \E_\pi[R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}\mid S_t=s] \\ &= \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\Big[r(s,a,s')+\gamma\,\E_\pi[G_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}=s']\Big] \\ &= \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\Big[r(s,a,s')+\gamma\, v_\pi(s')\Big]. \end{aligned}vπ​(s)​=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s]=Eπ​[Rt+1​+γGt+1​∣St​=s]=a∑​π(a∣s)s′∑​p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γEπ​[Gt+1​∣St+1​=s′]]=a∑​π(a∣s)s′∑​p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γvπ​(s′)].​ The first step sums over the first action (weighted by the policy) and over the next state (weighted by the dynamics). The last step uses the Markov property: given St+1=s′S_{t+1}=s'St+1​=s′, the expected future return does not depend on how we got there, so it is vπ(s′)v_\pi(s')vπ​(s′) by definition. Doing the same for qπq_\piqπ​: qπ(s,a)=∑s′p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γ∑a′π(a′∣s′) qπ(s′,a′)].q_\pi(s,a)=\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\Big[r(s,a,s')+\gamma\sum_{a'}\pi(a'\mid s')\,q_\pi(s',a')\Big].qπ​(s,a)=s′∑​p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γa′∑​π(a′∣s′)qπ​(s′,a′)].

In words: the value of a state is the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the successor. For a finite MDP this is a system of ∣S∣|\mathcal S|∣S∣ linear equations, vπ=rπ+γPπvπ\boldsymbol v_\pi=\boldsymbol r_\pi+\gamma\mathbf P_\pi\boldsymbol v_\pivπ​=rπ​+γPπ​vπ​, with the unique solution vπ=(I−γPπ)−1rπ\boldsymbol v_\pi=(\mathbf I-\gamma\mathbf P_\pi)^{-1}\boldsymbol r_\pivπ​=(I−γPπ​)−1rπ​ (the inverse exists for γ<1\gamma<1γ<1 because Pπ\mathbf P_\piPπ​ is a stochastic matrix, whose eigenvalues have modulus at most one). Direct solution costs O(∣S∣3)O(|\mathcal S|^3)O(∣S∣3), so for larger problems we iterate instead.

Optimality. A policy π\piπ is at least as good as π′\pi'π′ if vπ(s)≥vπ′(s)v_\pi(s)\ge v_{\pi'}(s)vπ​(s)≥vπ′​(s) for all sss. For finite MDPs there is always at least one optimal policy, and all optimal policies share the same optimal value functions v∗(s)=max⁡πvπ(s)v_*(s)=\max_\pi v_\pi(s)v∗​(s)=maxπ​vπ​(s) and q∗(s,a)=max⁡πqπ(s,a)q_*(s,a)=\max_\pi q_\pi(s,a)q∗​(s,a)=maxπ​qπ​(s,a). Because an optimal policy must pick the best action in every state, the expectation over the policy in the Bellman equation becomes a maximum:

v∗(s)=max⁡a∑s′p(s′∣s,a)[r+γv∗(s′)],q∗(s,a)=∑s′p(s′∣s,a)[r+γmax⁡a′q∗(s′,a′)].v_*(s)=\max_a\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r+\gamma v_*(s')\big],\qquad q_*(s,a)=\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\Big[r+\gamma\max_{a'}q_*(s',a')\Big].v∗​(s)=amax​s′∑​p(s′∣s,a)[r+γv∗​(s′)],q∗​(s,a)=s′∑​p(s′∣s,a)[r+γa′max​q∗​(s′,a′)].

These are the Bellman optimality equations. They are nonlinear (because of the max) and, crucially, once you know q∗q_*q∗​ the optimal policy is trivial to read off: act greedily, π∗(s)=arg max⁡aq∗(s,a)\pi_*(s)=\argmax_a q_*(s,a)π∗​(s)=argmaxa​q∗​(s,a). This is why so much of RL is about estimating q∗q_*q∗​.

Contraction view

Define the Bellman optimality operator (Tv)(s)=max⁡a∑s′p(s′∣s,a)[r+γv(s′)](\mathcal T v)(s)=\max_a\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)[r+\gamma v(s')](Tv)(s)=maxa​∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)[r+γv(s′)]. For any two value functions, ∥Tv−Tw∥∞≤γ∥v−w∥∞\norm{\mathcal Tv-\mathcal Tw}_\infty\le\gamma\norm{v-w}_\infty∥Tv−Tw∥∞​≤γ∥v−w∥∞​, i.e. T\mathcal TT is a γ\gammaγ-contraction in the max norm. By the Banach fixed-point theorem, repeated application converges to the unique fixed point v∗v_*v∗​, from any starting point, at a geometric rate γk\gamma^kγk. This single fact underpins value iteration and the convergence proofs of tabular Q-learning; its failure under function approximation is the subject of the deadly-triad section.

Dynamic programming: planning with a known model

Suppose, for now, you know the MDP exactly: ppp and rrr are given. Then finding a good policy is a planning problem, solved by dynamic programming (DP). DP matters for deep RL even though you rarely know the model, because model-free methods are best understood as sampled, approximate versions of DP updates.

Policy evaluation. To compute vπv_\pivπ​ iteratively, turn the Bellman expectation equation into an update rule: start from any v0v_0v0​ and repeatedly set vk+1(s)←∑aπ(a∣s)∑s′p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γvk(s′)].v_{k+1}(s)\leftarrow\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s')+\gamma v_k(s')\big].vk+1​(s)←a∑​π(a∣s)s′∑​p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γvk​(s′)]. This is also a γ\gammaγ-contraction, so vk→vπv_k\to v_\pivk​→vπ​.

Policy improvement. Given vπv_\pivπ​, form the greedy policy π′(s)=arg max⁡aqπ(s,a)\pi'(s)=\argmax_a q_\pi(s,a)π′(s)=argmaxa​qπ​(s,a). The policy improvement theorem says that π′\pi'π′ is at least as good as π\piπ: because acting greedily for one step and then following π\piπ is no worse than following π\piπ throughout, and the argument can be repeated at every subsequent step, vπ′≥vπv_{\pi'}\ge v_\pivπ′​≥vπ​ everywhere. If the improvement is zero the Bellman optimality equation holds and π\piπ is optimal.

Policy iteration alternates full evaluation and greedy improvement; in a finite MDP it terminates in a finite number of iterations at an optimal policy, typically in surprisingly few. Value iteration collapses the two steps by using the optimality equation as an update: vk+1(s)←max⁡a∑s′p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γvk(s′)].v_{k+1}(s)\leftarrow\max_a\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s')+\gamma v_k(s')\big].vk+1​(s)←amax​s′∑​p(s′∣s,a)[r(s,a,s′)+γvk​(s′)]. Each sweep costs O(∣S∣2∣A∣)O(|\mathcal S|^2|\mathcal A|)O(∣S∣2∣A∣). Generalized policy iteration (GPI) is Sutton and Barto's name for the unifying picture: an evaluation process pushes the value function toward vπv_\pivπ​, an improvement process pushes the policy toward greedy with respect to the value function, and the two chase each other to the optimum. Almost every algorithm below fits this pattern, with the exact steps replaced by sampled, partial ones.

pythonvalue_iteration.py
import numpy as np

# A 4x4 gridworld with a goal (bottom-right, reward +1, terminal) and a pit (reward -1, terminal).
# Actions: 0=up, 1=right, 2=down, 3=left. Moves into walls leave the agent in place.
# Dynamics are slippery: with prob 0.8 the intended move, 0.1 each for the two perpendicular moves.
H = W = 4
nS, nA, gamma = H * W, 4, 0.95
goal, pit = 15, 11
moves = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]

def move(s, a):
    r, c = divmod(s, W)
    dr, dc = moves[a]
    r2, c2 = min(max(r + dr, 0), H - 1), min(max(c + dc, 0), W - 1)
    return r2 * W + c2

P = np.zeros((nS, nA, nS))     # P[s, a, s'] transition tensor
R = np.zeros((nS, nA, nS))     # R[s, a, s'] reward tensor
for s in range(nS):
    for a in range(nA):
        if s in (goal, pit):
            P[s, a, s] = 1.0   # absorbing terminal states
            continue
        for a2, p in [(a, 0.8), ((a + 1) % 4, 0.1), ((a - 1) % 4, 0.1)]:
            s2 = move(s, a2)
            P[s, a, s2] += p
            R[s, a, s2] = 1.0 if s2 == goal else (-1.0 if s2 == pit else -0.04)  # small step cost

def value_iteration(tol=1e-8):
    V = np.zeros(nS)
    for k in range(1000):
        # Q[s, a] = sum_s' P[s,a,s'] (R[s,a,s'] + gamma V[s'])
        Q = (P * (R + gamma * V[None, None, :])).sum(axis=2)
        V_new = Q.max(axis=1)
        V_new[[goal, pit]] = 0.0             # terminal states have value zero
        if np.abs(V_new - V).max() < tol:
            return V_new, Q, k
        V = V_new
    return V, Q, k

V, Q, iters = value_iteration()
print(f"converged in {iters} sweeps")
print(np.round(V.reshape(H, W), 3))
print("greedy policy:")
print(np.array(list("^>v<"))[Q.argmax(axis=1)].reshape(H, W))

Run it and you will see values that decay smoothly with distance from the goal, with the greedy policy routing around the pit (not along the cheapest straight line) because of the slippery dynamics: this is the Bellman equation planning for noise.

InteractiveGridworld: value iteration and Q-learning side by side

DP has two limitations that motivate the rest of the week. It needs the model ppp, and each sweep touches every state, which is impossible for Go (∼10170\sim10^{170}∼10170 positions) or an image-based state space. The cure for both is to learn from sampled experience and to generalize across states with function approximation.

Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning

Without a model, the agent has only sampled transitions. Two basic ways to turn samples into value estimates differ in what they use as the learning target.

Monte Carlo (MC) prediction

The definition vπ(s)=E[Gt∣St=s]v_\pi(s)=\E[G_t\mid S_t=s]vπ​(s)=E[Gt​∣St​=s] suggests the plain statistical approach: run complete episodes, compute the realized return GtG_tGt​ from each visit to sss, and average. In incremental form, with a step size α\alphaα, V(St)←V(St)+α[Gt−V(St)].V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha\big[G_t-V(S_t)\big].V(St​)←V(St​)+α[Gt​−V(St​)]. The target GtG_tGt​ is an unbiased sample of vπ(St)v_\pi(S_t)vπ​(St​), but it has high variance, since it sums many random rewards, actions and transitions. MC also needs episodes to finish before any update, so it cannot learn online in continuing tasks.

Temporal-difference (TD) learning

TD learning replaces the unknown tail of the return with the current estimate. Using Gt=Rt+1+γGt+1G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}Gt​=Rt+1​+γGt+1​ and approximating E[Gt+1∣St+1]≈V(St+1)\E[G_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}]\approx V(S_{t+1})E[Gt+1​∣St+1​]≈V(St+1​) gives TD(0): V(St)←V(St)+α δt,δt=Rt+1+γV(St+1)−V(St).V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha\,\delta_t,\qquad \delta_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1})-V(S_t).V(St​)←V(St​)+αδt​,δt​=Rt+1​+γV(St+1​)−V(St​). The quantity δt\delta_tδt​ is the TD error: the difference between a one-step lookahead and the current prediction. The target Rt+1+γV(St+1)R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1})Rt+1​+γV(St+1​) is biased (it relies on a possibly wrong VVV), but it has low variance (only one random reward and one random transition) and it can update after every single step. This is bootstrapping: updating an estimate from another estimate. Bootstrapping is the source of most of RL's efficiency and, as we will see, most of its instability.

Method Needs model Update after Target Bias Variance
Dynamic programming yes each sweep full expectation over one step + VVV bootstraps none (exact)
Monte Carlo no end of episode GtG_tGt​ unbiased high
TD(0) no every step Rt+1+γV(St+1)R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1})Rt+1​+γV(St+1​) bootstraps low
nnn-step TD no after nnn steps Rt+1+⋯+γnV(St+n)R_{t+1}+\dots+\gamma^{n}V(S_{t+n})Rt+1​+⋯+γnV(St+n​) in between in between

The nnn-step return interpolates, and the λ\lambdaλ-return averages all of them with geometric weights (1−λ)λn−1(1-\lambda)\lambda^{n-1}(1−λ)λn−1. We will meet exactly this device again as GAE. In practice, TD methods usually learn faster than MC, which is the empirical result Sutton and Barto illustrate on a random-walk task and which the cliff example below also shows.

Control: SARSA and Q-learning

To act, we want qqq rather than vvv (it tells us which action is best without a model). Apply the TD idea to action values. SARSA (named after the tuple St,At,Rt+1,St+1,At+1S_t,A_t,R_{t+1},S_{t+1},A_{t+1}St​,At​,Rt+1​,St+1​,At+1​) is on-policy: it evaluates the policy that is generating the data, including its exploration: Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γ Q(St+1,At+1)−Q(St,At)].Q(S_t,A_t)\leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t)+\alpha\big[R_{t+1}+\gamma\, Q(S_{t+1},A_{t+1})-Q(S_t,A_t)\big].Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α[Rt+1​+γQ(St+1​,At+1​)−Q(St​,At​)]. Q-learning (Watkins, 1989) is off-policy: whatever action the behaviour policy takes next, it bootstraps from the best action, thereby estimating q∗q_*q∗​ directly: Q(St,At)←Q(St,At)+α[Rt+1+γmax⁡a′Q(St+1,a′)−Q(St,At)].Q(S_t,A_t)\leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t)+\alpha\big[R_{t+1}+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(S_{t+1},a')-Q(S_t,A_t)\big].Q(St​,At​)←Q(St​,At​)+α[Rt+1​+γa′max​Q(St+1​,a′)−Q(St​,At​)]. The one-token difference (Q(St+1,At+1)Q(S_{t+1},A_{t+1})Q(St+1​,At+1​) versus max⁡a′Q(St+1,a′)\max_{a'}Q(S_{t+1},a')maxa′​Q(St+1​,a′)) has real consequences. Off-policy learning means you can learn about the greedy policy while following an exploratory one, or learn from old data or from another agent's data. That freedom is what lets DQN reuse a replay buffer. With a decaying step size and every state-action pair visited infinitely often, tabular Q-learning converges to q∗q_*q∗​ (Watkins and Dayan, 1992).

The classic demonstration is cliff walking: a 4 by 12 grid where the bottom row between the start and the goal is a cliff (reward −100-100−100, reset to start), and every other step costs −1-1−1. Following an ε\varepsilonε-greedy policy, Q-learning learns the shortest path along the cliff edge, but during training the random exploratory moves occasionally push it over; SARSA, because it accounts for its own exploration in its targets, learns the longer, safer path.

pythoncliff.py
import numpy as np

H, W = 4, 12
START, GOAL = 3 * W, 3 * W + 11
moves = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]  # up, right, down, left

def step(s, a):
    r, c = divmod(s, W)
    dr, dc = moves[a]
    r, c = min(max(r + dr, 0), H - 1), min(max(c + dc, 0), W - 1)
    if r == 3 and 0 < c < 11:             # stepped into the cliff
        return START, -100.0, False
    return r * W + c, -1.0, (r * W + c == GOAL)

def train(algo, episodes=300, alpha=0.5, gamma=1.0, eps=0.1, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Q = np.zeros((H * W, 4))
    def act(s):                           # epsilon-greedy with random tie-breaking
        if rng.random() < eps:
            return int(rng.integers(4))
        return int(np.argmax(Q[s] + 1e-9 * rng.random(4)))
    returns = []
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, a, G = START, act(START), 0.0
        for _ in range(500):
            s2, r, done = step(s, a)
            a2 = act(s2)
            # Q-learning bootstraps from the greedy action; SARSA from the action actually chosen next
            boot = Q[s2].max() if algo == "q" else Q[s2, a2]
            target = r + (0.0 if done else gamma * boot)
            Q[s, a] += alpha * (target - Q[s, a])
            s, a, G = s2, a2, G + r
            if done:
                break
        returns.append(G)
    return np.array(returns)

for algo in ("q", "sarsa"):
    R = np.mean([train(algo, seed=k) for k in range(50)], axis=0)
    print(algo, "mean online return, last 100 episodes:", R[-100:].mean().round(1))

The lesson is general. On-policy methods value the policy they actually execute, exploration noise included. Off-policy methods value a different (usually greedy) target policy, so they find the better final policy but can behave worse while learning. If you were to anneal ε→0\varepsilon\to0ε→0, both would converge to the optimal path.

A bandit warm-up: the exploration-exploitation dilemma

Strip an MDP down to a single state and you get the multi-armed bandit: kkk actions ("arms"), each with an unknown mean reward q∗(a)q_*(a)q∗​(a). There is no state and no long-term consequence, so what remains is the pure exploration versus exploitation trade-off: pull the arm that looks best now (exploit), or pull another to learn whether it is better (explore). The simplest strategy is ε\varepsilonε-greedy: with probability ε\varepsilonε choose a random arm, otherwise choose the arm with the highest sample-mean estimate Q(a)Q(a)Q(a). The estimate is updated incrementally, Qn+1=Qn+1n(Rn−Qn)Q_{n+1}=Q_n+\frac1n(R_n-Q_n)Qn+1​=Qn​+n1​(Rn​−Qn​), which is the same "estimate ←\leftarrow← estimate + step ×\times× error" shape as every update in this chapter.

The ten-armed testbed (Sutton and Barto, Ch. 2) draws each q∗(a)∼N(0,1)q_*(a)\sim\mathcal N(0,1)q∗​(a)∼N(0,1) and rewards N(q∗(a),1)\mathcal N(q_*(a),1)N(q∗​(a),1). The greedy learner (ε=0\varepsilon=0ε=0) often locks on to a mediocre arm after a lucky early sample and never recovers; a small ε\varepsilonε keeps sampling and eventually finds the best arm. The next chart averages 1000 such randomly generated problems.

InteractiveBandit explorer: epsilon-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling

Two alternatives deserve a name. UCB1 (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer, 2002) adds an optimism bonus that shrinks as an arm is sampled more: choose arg max⁡a Q(a)+cln⁡t/N(a)\argmax_a\,Q(a)+c\sqrt{\ln t/N(a)}argmaxa​Q(a)+clnt/N(a)​. It explores arms whose value is uncertain rather than arms chosen at random. Thompson sampling (Thompson, 1933) keeps a posterior over each arm's mean, samples one value per arm from the posterior, and pulls the arm with the largest sample. Both achieve regret that grows only logarithmically with time, whereas fixed-ε\varepsilonε exploration has linear regret because it never stops exploring. We return to exploration in the deep setting in its own section, where counting visits is no longer possible and the ideas have to be approximated.

Function approximation and the deadly triad

Tables do not scale. An Atari frame is 210×160210\times160210×160 RGB pixels; the number of distinct states is astronomically large and the agent almost never sees the same state twice. We must generalize: represent q(s,a)q(s,a)q(s,a) by a parametric function q^(s,a;θ)\hat q(s,a;\boldsymbol\theta)q^​(s,a;θ), such as a neural network, so that experience in one state informs predictions in similar ones. The natural idea is to treat the TD target as a label and do gradient descent on the squared error. For a transition (s,a,r,s′)(s,a,r,s')(s,a,r,s′) the semi-gradient Q-learning update is θ←θ+α[r+γmax⁡a′q^(s′,a′;θ)−q^(s,a;θ)]∇θq^(s,a;θ).\boldsymbol\theta\leftarrow\boldsymbol\theta+\alpha\Big[r+\gamma\max_{a'}\hat q(s',a';\boldsymbol\theta)-\hat q(s,a;\boldsymbol\theta)\Big]\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\hat q(s,a;\boldsymbol\theta).θ←θ+α[r+γa′max​q^​(s′,a′;θ)−q^​(s,a;θ)]∇θ​q^​(s,a;θ). It is called a semi-gradient because the target contains θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ too, but we treat it as a constant when differentiating (in PyTorch: compute the target under torch.no_grad() or call .detach()). The true gradient of the squared Bellman error (the "residual gradient") also pushes the target toward the prediction, converges more reliably in theory, and in practice learns far slower and to worse solutions, so nobody uses it for deep RL.

Unlike supervised learning, this can diverge. Sutton and Barto identify the deadly triad: instability and divergence become possible when three ingredients are combined.

  1. Function approximation: generalization means that updating one state changes the values of many others, including the very states whose values we bootstrap from.
  2. Bootstrapping: targets depend on the current estimate, so errors feed back on themselves instead of being anchored by true returns.
  3. Off-policy training: the data distribution does not match the distribution of the policy being evaluated, so there is no guarantee that the states where errors grow are the states that get corrected.

Any two of the three are fine. Tabular Q-learning (no approximation) converges. On-policy TD with linear approximation converges. Monte Carlo (no bootstrapping) with off-policy data is well behaved. Baird's counterexample (1995), a seven-state MDP with a linear value function, makes off-policy semi-gradient TD diverge to infinity from a harmless starting point, and it takes a couple of dozen lines to reproduce. For deep Q-learning, which has all three, divergence takes the form of Q-values that explode, oscillate, or quietly become wildly overestimated. Everything in the DQN section is a practical recipe for keeping the triad under control: break the correlations in the data (replay), keep the target from moving every step (target network), and tame the scale of errors (Huber loss, gradient clipping, reward clipping).

Why does bootstrapping with a function approximator go wrong?

Imagine a value network that has slightly overestimated V(s′)V(s')V(s′). Because the network generalizes, the overestimate leaks onto the neighbours of s′s's′, including sss. The TD target for sss is r+γV(s′)r+\gamma V(s')r+γV(s′), which is now too high, so we push V(s)V(s)V(s) up, which leaks onto s′s's′ again. With γ\gammaγ near 1 and a poorly chosen feature space this feedback loop can have gain above one, and the error grows geometrically. With a table there is no leakage and the contraction property guarantees the loop dies out. Off-policy data makes it worse because nothing forces us to visit the states where the overestimate is wrong and get a corrective negative sample.

Deep Q-networks (DQN)

Before 2013 it was widely believed that combining Q-learning with a neural network was too unstable to be useful, despite isolated successes such as Tesauro's TD-Gammon (1992) in backgammon. DQN (Mnih et al., 2013 workshop paper; Nature, 2015, "Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning") showed that a single convolutional network with a fixed architecture and hyper-parameters could learn to play dozens of Atari 2600 games from raw pixels and the score alone, reaching human-level performance on many of them. Its network takes a stack of the last four preprocessed frames (grayscale, 84×8484\times8484×84) and outputs one Q-value per discrete action, so a single forward pass scores every action; this is cheaper than feeding (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) pairs and makes the max⁡a′\max_{a'}maxa′​ trivial.

Experience replay

A raw stream of experience is a poor training set: consecutive transitions are strongly correlated (almost identical frames), and the data distribution shifts as the policy changes, so gradient descent on the most recent transitions chases its own tail and can forget earlier behaviour. Experience replay (Lin, 1992) stores the last NNN transitions (st,at,rt+1,st+1,dt+1)(s_t,a_t,r_{t+1},s_{t+1},d_{t+1})(st​,at​,rt+1​,st+1​,dt+1​) in a buffer (N=106N=10^6N=106 in DQN) and trains on minibatches sampled uniformly at random. This (i) decorrelates the minibatch, making it closer to the i.i.d. assumption of SGD, (ii) reuses each transition many times, making learning far more sample-efficient, and (iii) averages over a long history of behaviours, smoothing the data distribution. It also requires off-policy learning: the buffer holds data from old policies, which is one more reason Q-learning (not SARSA) is the right base algorithm.

The target network

Plain semi-gradient Q-learning has the target and the prediction computed by the same, rapidly changing parameters, which is the feedback loop above. DQN keeps a second copy of the network with parameters θ−\boldsymbol\theta^-θ− used only to compute targets, and refreshes it from the online network every CCC steps (10,000 in the original Atari setup). The loss for a minibatch B\mathcal BB of transitions is L(θ)=1∣B∣∑(s,a,r,s′,d)∈B(r+γ(1−d)max⁡a′q^(s′,a′;θ−)⏟y, treated as constant−q^(s,a;θ))2.\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\theta)=\frac1{|\mathcal B|}\sum_{(s,a,r,s',d)\in\mathcal B}\Big(\underbrace{r+\gamma(1-d)\max_{a'}\hat q(s',a';\boldsymbol\theta^-)}_{y,\ \text{treated as constant}}-\hat q(s,a;\boldsymbol\theta)\Big)^2.L(θ)=∣B∣1​(s,a,r,s′,d)∈B∑​(y, treated as constantr+γ(1−d)a′max​q^​(s′,a′;θ−)​​−q^​(s,a;θ))2. For a period of CCC steps the regression targets are stationary, turning the moving-target problem into a sequence of ordinary supervised problems. Many modern implementations use a soft (Polyak) update, θ−←τθ+(1−τ)θ−\boldsymbol\theta^-\leftarrow\tau\boldsymbol\theta+(1-\tau)\boldsymbol\theta^-θ−←τθ+(1−τ)θ− with τ≈0.005\tau\approx0.005τ≈0.005, every step, which achieves the same stabilization more smoothly. The original paper also clipped rewards to [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] and clipped the TD error (equivalent to the Huber loss), which prevents a rare large reward from producing enormous gradients.

The full algorithm

text
Initialize online network Q(s,a;θ), target network Q(s,a;θ⁻) ← θ, replay buffer D
for each environment step t:
    with prob ε_t choose a random action, else a = argmax_a Q(s_t, a; θ)    # ε annealed 1.0 -> 0.05 or 0.01
    execute a, observe r, s_{t+1}, done; store (s_t, a, r, s_{t+1}, done) in D
    if t >= learning_starts and t % train_freq == 0:
        sample minibatch of B transitions from D
        y = r + γ (1 - done) max_a' Q(s', a'; θ⁻)
        minimize Huber(y - Q(s, a; θ)) with Adam / RMSProp, clip gradient norm
    every C steps (or softly each step): θ⁻ ← θ

Typical Atari hyper-parameters: replay 1M, minibatch 32, γ=0.99\gamma=0.99γ=0.99, ε\varepsilonε from 1.0 to 0.1 over the first million frames, learning rate 2.5×10−42.5\times10^{-4}2.5×10−4 (RMSProp in the original), update every 4 agent steps. The lab below uses a smaller version on CartPole with a two-hidden-layer MLP.

Atari and the arcade learning environment

The Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al., 2013, JAIR) exposed Atari 2600 games as an RL benchmark. DQN's headline result in the 2015 Nature paper was reaching more than 75% of a professional human tester's score on 29 of 49 games with a single set of hyper-parameters. Later work (Rainbow, Hessel et al., 2018, AAAI) combined six DQN extensions, and the field's benchmark moved to measuring sample efficiency (for example Atari 100k) since DQN needs tens of millions of frames, equivalent to many days of human play.

Improving DQN: Double, Dueling and prioritized replay

DQN has well-understood weaknesses. Three of the most useful repairs each address one specific failure and are cheap to add.

Double DQN: fixing overestimation

The target max⁡a′q^(s′,a′)\max_{a'}\hat q(s',a')maxa′​q^​(s′,a′) takes a maximum over noisy estimates. Even if each estimate is unbiased, the expected maximum of noisy values is larger than the maximum of the expected values: E[max⁡aXa]≥max⁡aE[Xa]\E[\max_a X_a]\ge\max_a\E[X_a]E[maxa​Xa​]≥maxa​E[Xa​] (Jensen's inequality for the convex max function). With a network full of approximation error, Q-learning is therefore systematically optimistic, and the optimism is then bootstrapped and propagated. The same network both selects the action that looks best and evaluates it, so selection noise and evaluation noise are positively correlated: an action is picked precisely because its error happens to be positive.

Double Q-learning (van Hasselt, 2010) decouples the two roles. Double DQN (van Hasselt, Guez and Silver, 2016) does it with the machinery already at hand: select the action with the online network, evaluate it with the target network: y=r+γ(1−d)  q^(s′, arg max⁡a′q^(s′,a′;θ); θ−).y=r+\gamma(1-d)\;\hat q\Big(s',\ \argmax_{a'}\hat q(s',a';\boldsymbol\theta);\ \boldsymbol\theta^-\Big).y=r+γ(1−d)q^​(s′, a′argmax​q^​(s′,a′;θ); θ−). The change is one line of code, costs nothing, and gave large improvements on several Atari games where vanilla DQN's value estimates were wildly too high. It is not an unbiased estimator (it can underestimate slightly), but the bias is much smaller and less harmful.

pythondouble_dqn_target.py
import torch

def dqn_targets(online, target, r, s_next, done, gamma, double=True):
    """Return TD targets y of shape (B,). All inputs are batched tensors:
    r (B,), s_next (B, obs_dim), done (B,) with values 0.0 or 1.0."""
    with torch.no_grad():                                   # targets are constants in the loss
        q_next_target = target(s_next)                      # (B, n_actions)
        if double:
            a_star = online(s_next).argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True)    # select with ONLINE net
            q_next = q_next_target.gather(1, a_star).squeeze(1)    # evaluate with TARGET net
        else:
            q_next = q_next_target.max(dim=1).values               # vanilla DQN: max of target
        return r + gamma * (1.0 - done) * q_next

Dueling DQN: separate what the state is worth from what the action adds

In many states the choice of action barely matters (the car is not near an obstacle; the pole is nearly upright), yet a standard Q-network must learn q(s,a)q(s,a)q(s,a) separately for every action. The dueling architecture (Wang et al., 2016) shares the convolutional or MLP trunk and then splits into two heads: a scalar value stream V(s)V(s)V(s) and an advantage stream A(s,a)A(s,a)A(s,a) with one output per action, recombined as Q(s,a)=V(s)+(A(s,a)−1∣A∣∑a′A(s,a′)).Q(s,a)=V(s)+\Big(A(s,a)-\frac1{|\mathcal A|}\sum_{a'}A(s,a')\Big).Q(s,a)=V(s)+(A(s,a)−∣A∣1​a′∑​A(s,a′)). The decomposition alone is not identifiable (add a constant to VVV and subtract it from every AAA and QQQ is unchanged), so the mean advantage is subtracted, forcing the advantages to be centred and giving VVV a unique meaning. The practical gain is that every update, whichever action was taken, trains the shared value stream, so V(s)V(s)V(s) is learnt faster and generalizes across actions, which matters most when there are many actions with similar values. The dueling head is a change to the network only and composes with Double DQN and replay.

Prioritized experience replay

Uniform sampling treats every stored transition as equally useful. A transition with a large TD error (a surprising outcome) has a lot to teach; one the network already predicts well has little. Prioritized experience replay (Schaul et al., 2016) samples transition iii with probability P(i)=piα∑kpkα,pi=∣δi∣+ϵ,P(i)=\frac{p_i^{\alpha}}{\sum_k p_k^{\alpha}},\qquad p_i=|\delta_i|+\epsilon,P(i)=∑k​pkα​piα​​,pi​=∣δi​∣+ϵ, where δi\delta_iδi​ is the TD error recorded the last time iii was used, ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0 ensures every transition has some chance, and α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1]α∈[0,1] interpolates between uniform (α=0\alpha=0α=0) and greedy prioritization. Sampling non-uniformly changes the expected gradient, i.e. it introduces bias, so the loss for each sampled transition is multiplied by an importance-sampling weight wi=(1NP(i))βw_i=\big(\tfrac1{N P(i)}\big)^{\beta}wi​=(NP(i)1​)β (normalized by the largest weight), with β\betaβ annealed to 1 over training. Implementations use a sum-tree so that sampling and priority updates cost O(log⁡N)O(\log N)O(logN). New transitions are inserted with maximal priority so they are seen at least once. Prioritization usually speeds up learning on Atari substantially, but it adds hyper-parameters (α,β\alpha,\betaα,β) and can hurt on noisy-reward tasks, where TD error reflects irreducible noise rather than learnable surprise.

Other extensions and Rainbow

Other widely used improvements: multi-step returns (nnn-step targets, which cut bootstrap bias at the cost of some off-policy bias), distributional RL (C51, Bellemare et al., 2017, learns the whole return distribution, not just its mean), noisy networks (Fortunato et al., 2018, learned parameter noise for exploration instead of ε\varepsilonε-greedy). Hessel et al. (2018) combined these six extensions (Double, Dueling, prioritized, multi-step, distributional, noisy) in Rainbow and ablated them, finding that prioritized replay and multi-step returns mattered most and that the combination was better than any single one.

Policy-gradient methods

Value-based methods learn qqq and derive a policy by maximizing over actions. That has three limits. The max⁡a\max_amaxa​ is awkward or expensive when actions are continuous. The greedy policy is deterministic, but some problems (rock-paper-scissors, partially observed environments) need a stochastic optimal policy. And a small change in qqq can cause an abrupt change in the greedy action, which is part of what makes the triad dangerous. Policy-gradient methods parameterize the policy directly, πθ(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a\mid s)πθ​(a∣s) (a softmax over action logits for discrete actions, a Gaussian with learned mean and standard deviation for continuous ones) and ascend the gradient of expected return, J(θ)=Eτ∼πθ[R(τ)],R(τ)=∑t=0T−1γtrt+1.J(\boldsymbol\theta)=\E_{\tau\sim\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}}\big[R(\tau)\big],\qquad R(\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t r_{t+1}.J(θ)=Eτ∼πθ​​[R(τ)],R(τ)=t=0∑T−1​γtrt+1​. The challenge: JJJ depends on θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ through the distribution of trajectories, including the unknown environment dynamics, and sampling an action is not a differentiable operation. The policy gradient theorem shows how to get a gradient anyway, with no derivative of the dynamics needed.

The policy gradient theorem

Derivation: the log-derivative trick and the policy gradient

Write the probability of a trajectory as pθ(τ)=p(s0)∏t=0T−1πθ(at∣st) p(st+1∣st,at)p_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\tau)=p(s_0)\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a_t\mid s_t)\,p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)pθ​(τ)=p(s0​)∏t=0T−1​πθ​(at​∣st​)p(st+1​∣st​,at​). Then ∇θJ=∇θ∫pθ(τ)R(τ) dτ=∫pθ(τ) ∇θlog⁡pθ(τ) R(τ) dτ,\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}J=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\int p_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\tau)R(\tau)\,d\tau=\int p_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\tau)\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\log p_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\tau)\,R(\tau)\,d\tau,∇θ​J=∇θ​∫pθ​(τ)R(τ)dτ=∫pθ​(τ)∇θ​logpθ​(τ)R(τ)dτ, using the identity ∇p=p ∇log⁡p\nabla p=p\,\nabla\log p∇p=p∇logp (the log-derivative trick, also called the score-function or likelihood-ratio estimator). Dropping these terms gives the lower-variance form, the policy gradient theorem:   ∇θJ=Eτ∼πθ[∑t=0T−1∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)  Gt],Gt=∑k≥tγk−trk+1  \boxed{\;\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}J=\E_{\tau\sim\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a_t\mid s_t)\;G_t\Big],\qquad G_t=\sum_{k\ge t}\gamma^{k-t}r_{k+1}\;}∇θ​J=Eτ∼πθ​​[t=0∑T−1​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)Gt​],Gt​=k≥t∑​γk−trk+1​​ (up to a γt\gamma^tγt factor on each term which practical implementations drop; the omitted factor changes the gradient to one that is not the true gradient of the discounted objective but works well in practice). The general form is E[∇log⁡π(at∣st) Ψt]\E[\nabla\log\pi(a_t|s_t)\,\Psi_t]E[∇logπ(at​∣st​)Ψt​] for any Ψt\Psi_tΨt​ whose expectation given (st,at)(s_t,a_t)(st​,at​) is qπ(st,at)q_\pi(s_t,a_t)qπ​(st​,at​), up to a baseline: this is where the actor-critic family comes from.

Read the formula as a recipe: increase the log-probability of each action taken, in proportion to the return that followed it. Good outcomes make their actions more likely; bad outcomes make them less likely. In effect we are doing supervised learning on the policy's own samples, with the return as a per-sample weight.

REINFORCE

REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) is the Monte Carlo estimator of the theorem: sample trajectories by running πθ\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}πθ​, compute returns-to-go GtG_tGt​, and take a step along ∑t∇log⁡πθ(at∣st)Gt\sum_t\nabla\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a_t\mid s_t)G_t∑t​∇logπθ​(at​∣st​)Gt​. In PyTorch you implement it by minimizing the surrogate loss −∑tlog⁡πθ(at∣st) Gt-\sum_t\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a_t\mid s_t)\,G_t−∑t​logπθ​(at​∣st​)Gt​, whose gradient (with GtG_tGt​ treated as constant) is exactly the negative of the policy gradient estimate. REINFORCE is unbiased but its variance is large: the weight GtG_tGt​ is a sum of many random rewards, and a trajectory-level return provides a noisy signal about any individual action. With returns that are always positive (as in CartPole, where every step gives +1), every sampled action is pushed up, only by different amounts, and learning is slow and noisy.

Baselines

Subtracting a baseline b(st)b(s_t)b(st​) that does not depend on the action leaves the gradient unbiased but can reduce its variance sharply: ∇θJ=E[∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st) (Gt−b(st))].\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}J=\E\Big[\sum_t\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a_t\mid s_t)\,\big(G_t-b(s_t)\big)\Big].∇θ​J=E[t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)(Gt​−b(st​))]. Unbiasedness follows from the same identity as before: Ea∼π[∇log⁡π(a∣s) b(s)]=b(s) ∇∑aπ(a∣s)=0\E_{a\sim\pi}[\nabla\log\pi(a\mid s)\,b(s)]=b(s)\,\nabla\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)=0Ea∼π​[∇logπ(a∣s)b(s)]=b(s)∇∑a​π(a∣s)=0. The best simple choice is b(s)=vπ(s)b(s)=v_\pi(s)b(s)=vπ​(s), which makes the weight Gt−vπ(st)G_t-v_\pi(s_t)Gt​−vπ​(st​) an estimate of the advantage: actions are reinforced only when they did better than average from that state, and discouraged when worse. The sign of the update now carries information. In practice vπv_\pivπ​ is learned by a second network (the critic) trained by regression on the returns, and a cheap extra step is to normalize advantages within a batch to zero mean and unit variance.

pythonreinforce_numpy.py
import numpy as np

# REINFORCE with a learned baseline on a 1-D "walk to the goal" task, in pure NumPy.
# States 0..N; start at N//2; actions: left/right; reaching N gives +1, reaching 0 gives 0;
# each step costs 0.01. Policy: state-independent softmax over {left,right} parameterized by logits.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, gamma = 8, 0.99
theta = np.zeros((N + 1, 2))       # tabular policy logits per state
Vb = np.zeros(N + 1)               # learned baseline V(s)

def pi(s):
    z = np.exp(theta[s] - theta[s].max())
    return z / z.sum()

def episode():
    s, traj = N // 2, []
    while 0 < s < N and len(traj) < 200:
        a = rng.choice(2, p=pi(s))
        s2 = s + (1 if a == 1 else -1)
        r = 1.0 if s2 == N else -0.01
        traj.append((s, a, r)); s = s2
    return traj

lr_pi, lr_v, history = 0.1, 0.1, []
for it in range(2000):
    traj = episode()
    G, rets = 0.0, []
    for (_, _, r) in reversed(traj):               # returns-to-go G_t
        G = r + gamma * G
        rets.append(G)
    rets.reverse()
    for (s, a, _), Gt in zip(traj, rets):
        adv = Gt - Vb[s]                           # advantage estimate with baseline
        Vb[s] += lr_v * adv                        # critic: regress V(s) toward G_t
        grad_logp = -pi(s); grad_logp[a] += 1.0    # d log pi(a|s) / d logits for a softmax
        theta[s] += lr_pi * adv * grad_logp        # ascend along grad log pi * advantage
    history.append(sum(r for _, _, r in traj))
print("mean return, first 100 episodes:", np.mean(history[:100]).round(3))
print("mean return, last 100 episodes: ", np.mean(history[-100:]).round(3))
print("P(right) per state:", np.round([pi(s)[1] for s in range(1, N)], 2))

Running it prints roughly the following (exact numbers depend on the seed): the average return rises from about 0.87 to about 0.97 and the learnt policy moves right with high probability in most states.

Actor-critic methods

REINFORCE with a baseline still uses a full Monte Carlo return as the weight, so its variance grows with the episode length and it cannot update until an episode ends. Actor-critic methods apply the TD idea from earlier to the policy-gradient weight. They keep two function approximators: an actor πθ(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a\mid s)πθ​(a∣s) and a critic Vϕ(s)V_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s)Vϕ​(s). Replace the Monte Carlo return by a one-step bootstrapped estimate, Gt−V(st)  →  rt+1+γVϕ(st+1)−Vϕ(st)=δtG_t-V(s_t)\;\to\;r_{t+1}+\gamma V_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s_t)=\delta_tGt​−V(st​)→rt+1​+γVϕ​(st+1​)−Vϕ​(st​)=δt​, the TD error. Then the actor's update is Δθ∝δt ∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st),\Delta\boldsymbol\theta\propto\delta_t\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a_t\mid s_t),Δθ∝δt​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​), and the critic is trained by regression to the bootstrapped target, LV=(rt+1+γ(1−d)Vϕ(st+1)−Vϕ(st))2\mathcal L_V=\big(r_{t+1}+\gamma(1-d)V_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s_t)\big)^2LV​=(rt+1​+γ(1−d)Vϕ​(st+1​)−Vϕ​(st​))2 (target held constant). The critic's TD error is a sample of the advantage: E[δt∣st,at]=qπ(st,at)−vπ(st)\E[\delta_t\mid s_t,a_t]=q_\pi(s_t,a_t)-v_\pi(s_t)E[δt​∣st​,at​]=qπ​(st​,at​)−vπ​(st​) when V=vπV=v_\piV=vπ​. We have traded the unbiased, high-variance MC weight for a low-variance, biased (because VϕV_{\boldsymbol\phi}Vϕ​ is imperfect) TD weight. The two networks usually share a trunk and have separate output heads, with a combined loss L=−log⁡πθ(at∣st) A^t⏟policy+cv(Vϕ(st)−V^ttarget)2⏟value−ceH[πθ(⋅∣st)]⏟entropy bonus,\mathcal L=\underbrace{-\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a_t\mid s_t)\,\hat A_t}_{\text{policy}}+c_v\underbrace{\big(V_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s_t)-\hat V^{\text{target}}_t\big)^2}_{\text{value}}-c_e\underbrace{\mathcal H\big[\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\cdot\mid s_t)\big]}_{\text{entropy bonus}},L=policy−logπθ​(at​∣st​)A^t​​​+cv​value(Vϕ​(st​)−V^ttarget​)2​​−ce​entropy bonusH[πθ​(⋅∣st​)]​​, with typical coefficients cv≈0.5c_v\approx0.5cv​≈0.5 and ce≈0.01c_e\approx0.01ce​≈0.01. The entropy bonus discourages the policy from collapsing to a deterministic one too early and is the simplest on-policy exploration device.

A2C and A3C

Training an actor-critic from a single stream of consecutive transitions gives strongly correlated updates; with no replay buffer (the method is on-policy, so old data is invalid) we need a different decorrelation device. A3C (Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic, Mnih et al., 2016) runs many CPU workers, each with its own copy of the environment and a local copy of the network. Each worker collects a short rollout (for example 5 steps), computes nnn-step advantages, and pushes its gradients asynchronously to a shared parameter server. Because workers explore different parts of the state space at different times, the gradient stream is decorrelated, and A3C matched or beat DQN on Atari in less wall-clock time on CPUs alone. A2C is the synchronous variant that OpenAI's baselines popularized: all workers step together, a single batch of transitions from NNN parallel environments is assembled, and one gradient step is taken. It is simpler, deterministic, and makes better use of a GPU, and it was found to work equally well in practice, so A2C is the standard today. The NNN parallel environments are what provides the batch diversity that replay provides in DQN.

Generalized advantage estimation (GAE)

How many steps should the advantage look ahead? One step gives low variance and high bias (the critic is trusted completely); a full Monte Carlo return gives no critic bias and high variance. GAE (Schulman et al., 2016) provides a dial between the two with a single parameter λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]λ∈[0,1], by taking an exponentially weighted average of all kkk-step advantage estimates.

Derivation: GAE

Let δt=rt+1+γV(st+1)−V(st)\delta_t=r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)δt​=rt+1​+γV(st+1​)−V(st​) be the TD error. The kkk-step advantage estimate is A^t(k)=∑l=0k−1γlrt+l+1+γkV(st+k)−V(st).\hat A_t^{(k)}=\sum_{l=0}^{k-1}\gamma^l r_{t+l+1}+\gamma^kV(s_{t+k})-V(s_t).A^t(k)​=l=0∑k−1​γlrt+l+1​+γkV(st+k​)−V(st​). Telescoping shows that it equals a discounted sum of TD errors. Writing ∑l=0k−1γlδt+l=∑l=0k−1γl(rt+l+1+γV(st+l+1)−V(st+l))\sum_{l=0}^{k-1}\gamma^l\delta_{t+l}=\sum_{l=0}^{k-1}\gamma^l\big(r_{t+l+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+l+1})-V(s_{t+l})\big)∑l=0k−1​γlδt+l​=∑l=0k−1​γl(rt+l+1​+γV(st+l+1​)−V(st+l​)), the value terms cancel pairwise except the endpoints, leaving A^t(k)=∑l=0k−1γlδt+l.\hat A_t^{(k)}=\sum_{l=0}^{k-1}\gamma^l\delta_{t+l}.A^t(k)​=l=0∑k−1​γlδt+l​. So A^t(1)=δt\hat A_t^{(1)}=\delta_tA^t(1)​=δt​ (low variance, biased) and A^t(∞)=∑l≥0γlδt+l=Gt−V(st)\hat A_t^{(\infty)}=\sum_{l\ge0}\gamma^l\delta_{t+l}=G_t-V(s_t)A^t(∞)​=∑l≥0​γlδt+l​=Gt​−V(st​) (the Monte Carlo advantage: unbiased, high variance). GAE takes the exponentially weighted average with weights (1−λ)λk−1(1-\lambda)\lambda^{k-1}(1−λ)λk−1: A^tGAE(γ,λ)=(1−λ)(A^t(1)+λA^t(2)+λ2A^t(3)+⋯)=(1−λ)(δt+λ(δt+γδt+1)+λ2(δt+γδt+1+γ2δt+2)+⋯).\begin{aligned} \hat A_t^{\text{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}&=(1-\lambda)\big(\hat A_t^{(1)}+\lambda\hat A_t^{(2)}+\lambda^2\hat A_t^{(3)}+\cdots\big)\\ &=(1-\lambda)\big(\delta_t+\lambda(\delta_t+\gamma\delta_{t+1})+\lambda^2(\delta_t+\gamma\delta_{t+1}+\gamma^2\delta_{t+2})+\cdots\big). \end{aligned}A^tGAE(γ,λ)​​=(1−λ)(A^t(1)​+λA^t(2)​+λ2A^t(3)​+⋯)=(1−λ)(δt​+λ(δt​+γδt+1​)+λ2(δt​+γδt+1​+γ2δt+2​)+⋯).​ Collect the coefficient of each δt+l\delta_{t+l}δt+l​: it is (1−λ)γl(λl+λl+1+⋯ )=(1−λ)γlλl/(1−λ)=(γλ)l(1-\lambda)\gamma^l(\lambda^l+\lambda^{l+1}+\cdots)=(1-\lambda)\gamma^l\lambda^l/(1-\lambda)=(\gamma\lambda)^l(1−λ)γl(λl+λl+1+⋯)=(1−λ)γlλl/(1−λ)=(γλ)l. Therefore A^tGAE(γ,λ)=∑l=0∞(γλ)l δt+l\boxed{\hat A_t^{\text{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(\gamma\lambda)^l\,\delta_{t+l}}A^tGAE(γ,λ)​=l=0∑∞​(γλ)lδt+l​​ This satisfies the cheap backward recursion A^t=δt+γλ A^t+1\hat A_t=\delta_t+\gamma\lambda\,\hat A_{t+1}A^t​=δt​+γλA^t+1​ with A^T=0\hat A_T=0A^T​=0 at the end of a rollout, which is how it is computed in code. The special cases are λ=0\lambda=0λ=0: A^t=δt\hat A_t=\delta_tA^t​=δt​, and λ=1\lambda=1λ=1: A^t=Gt−V(st)\hat A_t=G_t-V(s_t)A^t​=Gt​−V(st​).

If the critic were exact, every δt\delta_tδt​ would have zero conditional mean and GAE would be unbiased for any λ\lambdaλ; the bias comes entirely from critic error, and λ<1\lambda<1λ<1 damps how much of that error accumulates. The variance comes from the sum of many noisy rewards, which λ<1\lambda<1λ<1 truncates in effect after about 1/(1−γλ)1/(1-\gamma\lambda)1/(1−γλ) steps. Values around γ=0.99\gamma=0.99γ=0.99, λ=0.95\lambda=0.95λ=0.95 are standard defaults, but note that λ\lambdaλ is a bias-variance rule of thumb, not something with a theoretically optimal value. The following simulation makes the trade-off concrete.

The chart looks at a deliberately miscalibrated critic, so the "bias" here is the effect of the baseline's error being included in the estimate. The message, though, is the usual one: very large λ\lambdaλ makes the estimate sensitive to the accumulated noise of the whole episode, while small λ\lambdaλ stays close to one-step TD errors.

pythongae.py
import torch

def compute_gae(rewards, values, dones, last_value, gamma=0.99, lam=0.95):
    """rewards, values, dones: tensors of shape (T, N) from N parallel envs over T steps.
    last_value: (N,) critic value of the state after the final step (bootstrap).
    Returns advantages (T, N) and value targets (T, N)."""
    T, N = rewards.shape
    adv = torch.zeros_like(rewards)
    next_adv = torch.zeros(N)
    next_value = last_value
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        not_done = 1.0 - dones[t]                         # cut bootstrapping across episode ends
        delta = rewards[t] + gamma * next_value * not_done - values[t]
        next_adv = delta + gamma * lam * not_done * next_adv   # A_t = delta_t + gamma*lam*A_{t+1}
        adv[t] = next_adv
        next_value = values[t]
    returns = adv + values                                 # lambda-return targets for the critic
    return adv, returns

T, N = 5, 3
r = torch.ones(T, N); v = torch.zeros(T, N); d = torch.zeros(T, N)
adv, ret = compute_gae(r, v, d, last_value=torch.zeros(N))
print(adv[:, 0])   # with V = 0, r = 1: A_t = sum_l (gamma*lam)^l over the remaining steps: 4.44, 3.66, 2.83, 1.94, 1.0
InteractiveGAE: how lambda weights the TD errors

TRPO and PPO: safe policy updates

Policy-gradient methods have a problem that supervised learning does not. A step in parameter space of fixed size can change the policy a lot or a little depending on where you are, and a bad step ruins the data: the next batch is collected by the new, worse policy, so recovery is hard and a performance collapse can be permanent. We want to take the largest step that is guaranteed to be safe, and the right notion of "size" is measured in policy space (how much the action distribution changes), not parameter space.

The surrogate objective and the trust region

The starting point is an exact identity (Kakade and Langford, 2002) relating the performance of any two policies: J(π′)−J(π)=Eτ∼π′[∑tγtAπ(st,at)].J(\pi')-J(\pi)=\E_{\tau\sim\pi'}\Big[\sum_{t}\gamma^tA_\pi(s_t,a_t)\Big].J(π′)−J(π)=Eτ∼π′​[t∑​γtAπ​(st​,at​)]. The new policy is better exactly when, on states visited by the new policy, its actions have positive advantage under the old policy. The trouble is the expectation over π′\pi'π′'s state distribution, which we cannot sample before we have π′\pi'π′. If we approximate the state distribution by the old one (valid when the policies are close) and fix the action distribution with importance sampling, we get the surrogate objective Lπold(θ)=Es∼πold, a∼πold[πθ(a∣s)πold(a∣s) Aπold(s,a)]=E[rt(θ) A^t],rt(θ)=πθ(at∣st)πold(at∣st).L_{\pi_{\text{old}}}(\boldsymbol\theta)=\E_{s\sim\pi_{\text{old}},\,a\sim\pi_{\text{old}}}\Big[\frac{\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a\mid s)}\,A_{\pi_{\text{old}}}(s,a)\Big]=\E\big[r_t(\boldsymbol\theta)\,\hat A_t\big],\qquad r_t(\boldsymbol\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a_t\mid s_t)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a_t\mid s_t)}.Lπold​​(θ)=Es∼πold​,a∼πold​​[πold​(a∣s)πθ​(a∣s)​Aπold​​(s,a)]=E[rt​(θ)A^t​],rt​(θ)=πold​(at​∣st​)πθ​(at​∣st​)​. At θ=θold\boldsymbol\theta=\boldsymbol\theta_{\text{old}}θ=θold​ the ratio is 1 and the gradient of LLL equals the ordinary policy gradient, so LLL is a first-order-accurate local model of the true objective. It stops being accurate once the policies drift apart, which is why we need to constrain the step.

TRPO (Trust Region Policy Optimization, Schulman, Levine, Abbeel, Jordan and Moritz, 2015) maximizes the surrogate subject to a bound on the average KL divergence between the old and new policies: max⁡θ  Lπold(θ)s.t.DˉDKL(πold ∥ πθ)≤δ,\max_{\boldsymbol\theta}\;L_{\pi_{\text{old}}}(\boldsymbol\theta)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bar D_{\KL}\big(\pi_{\text{old}}\,\|\,\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}\big)\le\delta,θmax​Lπold​​(θ)s.t.DˉDKL​​(πold​∥πθ​)≤δ, with δ≈0.01\delta\approx0.01δ≈0.01. The paper derives a lower bound showing that, with a KL penalty, each such step guarantees monotonic improvement; the practical algorithm uses the constraint form with a larger step. Expanding LLL to first order and the KL to second order around θold\boldsymbol\theta_{\text{old}}θold​ gives a quadratic-constrained linear problem whose solution is the natural gradient step θ←θ+2δ/(g⊤F−1g)  F−1g\boldsymbol\theta\leftarrow\boldsymbol\theta+\sqrt{2\delta/(\boldsymbol g^\top\mathbf F^{-1}\boldsymbol g)}\;\mathbf F^{-1}\boldsymbol gθ←θ+2δ/(g⊤F−1g)​F−1g, where g=∇L\boldsymbol g=\nabla Lg=∇L and F\mathbf FF is the Fisher information matrix (the Hessian of the KL). TRPO never forms F\mathbf FF: it solves Fx=g\mathbf F\boldsymbol x=\boldsymbol gFx=g by conjugate gradient with Fisher-vector products, then does a backtracking line search to enforce the KL constraint and an actual improvement of the surrogate. It is principled and reliable but fiddly to implement, awkward with shared policy-value networks and with dropout or other stochastic layers, and expensive per update.

PPO: a first-order approximation of the trust region

Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman, Wolski, Dhariwal, Radford and Klimov, 2017) obtains much of TRPO's stability using nothing but a clipped objective and plain minibatch SGD with Adam, so that several epochs of updates can be run on each batch of data. The PPO-Clip objective is LCLIP(θ)=Et[min⁡(rt(θ)A^t, clip⁡(rt(θ), 1−ϵ, 1+ϵ)A^t)],ϵ≈0.1 to 0.3.L^{\text{CLIP}}(\boldsymbol\theta)=\E_t\Big[\min\Big(r_t(\boldsymbol\theta)\hat A_t,\ \operatorname{clip}\big(r_t(\boldsymbol\theta),\,1-\epsilon,\,1+\epsilon\big)\hat A_t\Big)\Big],\qquad\epsilon\approx0.1\text{ to }0.3.LCLIP(θ)=Et​[min(rt​(θ)A^t​, clip(rt​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^t​)],ϵ≈0.1 to 0.3. To see how it works, consider the two signs of the advantage.

  • A^t>0\hat A_t>0A^t​>0 (the action was better than expected). We want rtr_trt​ to increase. The objective is min⁡(rt, 1+ϵ)A^t\min(r_t,\,1+\epsilon)\hat A_tmin(rt​,1+ϵ)A^t​: it grows with rtr_trt​ until rt=1+ϵr_t=1+\epsilonrt​=1+ϵ and is flat afterwards. Once the policy has made that action 1+ϵ1+\epsilon1+ϵ times as likely, the gradient vanishes and there is no incentive to push further.
  • A^t<0\hat A_t<0A^t​<0 (the action was worse than expected). We want rtr_trt​ to decrease. The objective is max⁡(rt, 1−ϵ) A^t\max(r_t,\,1-\epsilon)\,\hat A_tmax(rt​,1−ϵ)A^t​ in effect (min⁡\minmin with a negative factor flips): it improves as rtr_trt​ falls until rt=1−ϵr_t=1-\epsilonrt​=1−ϵ and is flat below that.

The min⁡\minmin has a subtle and important role: it makes the objective a pessimistic lower bound of the unclipped surrogate. If the ratio has moved in the wrong direction (e.g. rt<1−ϵr_t<1-\epsilonrt​<1−ϵ for a positive-advantage action: the update made a good action less likely), the unclipped term is the smaller one, so it is used and the gradient is not zeroed; PPO does not hide mistakes by clipping them away. The clip therefore removes only the incentive to move beyond the trust region, in the favourable direction.

InteractivePPO clipping explorer: objective, gradient and trust region
Full PPO loss

In practice PPO minimizes the negative of LPPO=Et[LtCLIP−cv(Vϕ(st)−V^ttarg)2+ce H[πθ(⋅∣st)]],L^{\text{PPO}}=\E_t\Big[L^{\text{CLIP}}_t-c_v\big(V_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s_t)-\hat V_t^{\text{targ}}\big)^2+c_e\,\mathcal H\big[\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\cdot\mid s_t)\big]\Big],LPPO=Et​[LtCLIP​−cv​(Vϕ​(st​)−V^ttarg​)2+ce​H[πθ​(⋅∣st​)]], with A^t\hat A_tA^t​ from GAE and V^ttarg=A^t+Vold(st)\hat V^{\text{targ}}_t=\hat A_t+V_{\text{old}}(s_t)V^ttarg​=A^t​+Vold​(st​). One iteration: collect TTT steps from each of NNN parallel environments (for example N×T=2048N\times T=2048N×T=2048 samples), compute advantages with GAE, then run KKK epochs (commonly 3 to 10) of minibatch SGD on that fixed batch, and discard it. Common additions are advantage normalization per minibatch, gradient-norm clipping (0.5), learning-rate annealing, and (optionally) early stopping an iteration when the sampled KL to the old policy exceeds a threshold.

pythonppo_loss.py
import torch

def ppo_loss(new_logp, old_logp, adv, values, returns, entropy,
             clip_eps=0.2, c_v=0.5, c_e=0.01):
    """All tensors have shape (B,). new_logp: log pi_theta(a|s) under the current policy;
    old_logp: log-probs recorded when data was collected (no grad); adv: advantages;
    values: current critic outputs; returns: value targets; entropy: per-sample policy entropy."""
    adv = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)           # normalize advantages per minibatch
    ratio = torch.exp(new_logp - old_logp)                  # r_t(theta) computed in log space
    unclipped = ratio * adv
    clipped = torch.clamp(ratio, 1 - clip_eps, 1 + clip_eps) * adv
    policy_loss = -torch.min(unclipped, clipped).mean()     # maximize the pessimistic bound
    value_loss = 0.5 * (values - returns).pow(2).mean()
    approx_kl = (old_logp - new_logp).mean()                # cheap diagnostic of policy drift
    clip_frac = ((ratio - 1).abs() > clip_eps).float().mean()   # fraction of clipped samples
    loss = policy_loss + c_v * value_loss - c_e * entropy.mean()
    return loss, {"kl": approx_kl.item(), "clipfrac": clip_frac.item()}

# smoke test with random data
B = 64
nl, ol = torch.randn(B) * 0.05, torch.zeros(B)
loss, info = ppo_loss(nl, ol, torch.randn(B), torch.randn(B), torch.randn(B), torch.full((B,), 0.69))
print(loss.item(), info)

PPO is the workhorse of deep RL because it is simple, robust to hyper-parameters (compared with other methods), and works for discrete and continuous actions, for games, robotics and language models. A large study of implementation details (Engstrom et al., 2020, "Implementation Matters in Deep Policy Gradients") found that much of PPO's advantage over TRPO is attributable to code-level optimizations (such as learning-rate annealing, value clipping, reward normalization and orthogonal initialization) rather than the clipping itself, and the clip does not strictly enforce a trust region (ratios can leave [1−ϵ,1+ϵ][1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon][1−ϵ,1+ϵ] after several epochs). A good rule: monitor approx_kl and clipfrac, not just the return. Healthy values are a KL of order 10−210^{-2}10−2 or smaller and a clip fraction of 0.1 to 0.3.

Continuous control: DDPG, TD3 and SAC

Robot joints, steering angles and trading sizes are continuous. DQN's max⁡aq^(s,a)\max_a\hat q(s,a)maxa​q^​(s,a) would require solving an optimization problem at every step. Policy-gradient methods handle continuous actions naturally with a Gaussian policy, but PPO is on-policy and therefore sample-hungry, a real cost when each sample is a physical robot second. The methods in this section are off-policy actor-critic algorithms: they keep a replay buffer like DQN, learn a Q-function qϕ(s,a)q_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s,a)qϕ​(s,a) that takes the action as an input, and train an actor to output actions that maximize it.

DDPG

Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (Lillicrap et al., 2016) builds on the deterministic policy gradient theorem (Silver et al., 2014). The actor is a deterministic function a=μθ(s)a=\mu_{\boldsymbol\theta}(s)a=μθ​(s) and the critic qϕ(s,a)q_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s,a)qϕ​(s,a) is trained with a DQN-style Bellman loss, with target networks for both: y=r+γ(1−d) qϕ−(s′,μθ−(s′)),L(ϕ)=E[(qϕ(s,a)−y)2].y=r+\gamma(1-d)\,q_{\boldsymbol\phi^-}\big(s',\mu_{\boldsymbol\theta^-}(s')\big),\qquad\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\phi)=\E\big[(q_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s,a)-y)^2\big].y=r+γ(1−d)qϕ−​(s′,μθ−​(s′)),L(ϕ)=E[(qϕ​(s,a)−y)2]. The max⁡a′\max_{a'}maxa′​ of Q-learning is replaced by evaluating the target actor's action. The actor ascends the critic: by the chain rule, ∇θJ≈Es∼D[∇aqϕ(s,a)∣a=μθ(s)  ∇θμθ(s)].\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}J\approx\E_{s\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\nabla_a q_{\boldsymbol\phi}(s,a)\big|_{a=\mu_{\boldsymbol\theta}(s)}\;\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\mu_{\boldsymbol\theta}(s)\Big].∇θ​J≈Es∼D​[∇a​qϕ​(s,a)​a=μθ​(s)​∇θ​μθ​(s)]. In code you simply backpropagate -q(s, mu(s)).mean() into the actor's parameters, with the critic's parameters excluded from that optimizer step. Because the policy is deterministic, exploration is added externally (Gaussian or Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise on the action), and targets are updated by Polyak averaging. DDPG is sample-efficient but notoriously brittle: it is sensitive to hyper-parameters, and the critic's overestimation errors are exploited by the actor, which learns to climb narrow peaks of the approximate Q-function that do not exist in reality.

TD3

Twin Delayed DDPG (Fujimoto, van Hoof and Meger, 2018) adds three fixes that target that exact failure.

  1. Clipped double-Q learning. Learn two critics qϕ1,qϕ2q_{\boldsymbol\phi_1},q_{\boldsymbol\phi_2}qϕ1​​,qϕ2​​ and use the smaller of the two target values, y=r+γ(1−d)min⁡i=1,2qϕi−(s′,a′)y=r+\gamma(1-d)\min_{i=1,2}q_{\boldsymbol\phi_i^-}(s',a')y=r+γ(1−d)mini=1,2​qϕi−​​(s′,a′). Taking the minimum counters the upward bias of a single estimate, as in the Double DQN analysis.
  2. Delayed policy updates. Update the actor (and the target networks) less often than the critics (e.g. one actor step per two critic steps), so the actor follows a critic that has had time to settle.
  3. Target policy smoothing. Add clipped noise to the target action, a′=clip⁡(μθ−(s′)+clip⁡(ε,−c,c), alow,ahigh)a'=\operatorname{clip}\big(\mu_{\boldsymbol\theta^-}(s')+\operatorname{clip}(\varepsilon,-c,c),\,a_{\text{low}},a_{\text{high}}\big)a′=clip(μθ−​(s′)+clip(ε,−c,c),alow​,ahigh​) with ε∼N(0,σ2)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)ε∼N(0,σ2), which regularizes the critic by forcing similar actions to have similar values and prevents the actor from exploiting sharp peaks.

TD3 is a strong, simple baseline for state-based continuous control.

SAC and the maximum-entropy objective

Soft Actor-Critic (Haarnoja, Zhou, Abbeel and Levine, 2018) changes the objective itself. In maximum-entropy RL the agent maximizes reward and the entropy of its policy: J(π)=Eτ∼π[∑tγt(r(st,at)+α H[π(⋅∣st)])],H[π(⋅∣s)]=−Ea∼πlog⁡π(a∣s).J(\pi)=\E_{\tau\sim\pi}\Big[\sum_{t}\gamma^t\Big(r(s_t,a_t)+\alpha\,\mathcal H\big[\pi(\cdot\mid s_t)\big]\Big)\Big],\qquad\mathcal H[\pi(\cdot\mid s)]=-\E_{a\sim\pi}\log\pi(a\mid s).J(π)=Eτ∼π​[t∑​γt(r(st​,at​)+αH[π(⋅∣st​)])],H[π(⋅∣s)]=−Ea∼π​logπ(a∣s). The temperature α>0\alpha>0α>0 sets the exchange rate between reward and randomness. Why add entropy? It builds exploration into the objective (the agent prefers to keep options open), it prevents premature collapse to a deterministic policy, it makes the learnt behaviour more robust (the agent learns many ways to solve a task, so perturbations hurt less), and it tends to give smoother, more stable optimization. In the soft setting the Bellman backup includes an entropy term in the target: y=r+γ(1−d)(min⁡i=1,2qϕi−(s′,a′)−αlog⁡πθ(a′∣s′)),a′∼πθ(⋅∣s′).y=r+\gamma(1-d)\Big(\min_{i=1,2}q_{\boldsymbol\phi_i^-}(s',a')-\alpha\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a'\mid s')\Big),\qquad a'\sim\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\cdot\mid s').y=r+γ(1−d)(i=1,2min​qϕi−​​(s′,a′)−αlogπθ​(a′∣s′)),a′∼πθ​(⋅∣s′). The actor is a stochastic Gaussian policy (squashed through tanh⁡\tanhtanh to respect action bounds) trained to minimize Lπ(θ)=Es∼D, a∼πθ[αlog⁡πθ(a∣s)−min⁡iqϕi(s,a)],\mathcal L_\pi(\boldsymbol\theta)=\E_{s\sim\mathcal D,\ a\sim\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}}\Big[\alpha\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a\mid s)-\min_iq_{\boldsymbol\phi_i}(s,a)\Big],Lπ​(θ)=Es∼D, a∼πθ​​[αlogπθ​(a∣s)−imin​qϕi​​(s,a)], that is, to produce actions that are valuable and high-entropy. This is differentiable through the sampled action by the reparameterization trick (Week 12): a=tanh⁡(μθ(s)+σθ(s)⊙ξ)a=\tanh(\mu_{\boldsymbol\theta}(s)+\sigma_{\boldsymbol\theta}(s)\odot\xi)a=tanh(μθ​(s)+σθ​(s)⊙ξ), ξ∼N(0,I)\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,\mathbf I)ξ∼N(0,I). In the follow-up paper (Haarnoja et al., 2018b) the temperature is learnt automatically by treating the entropy as a constraint: α\alphaα is adjusted by gradient descent on α(−log⁡π(a∣s)−Hˉ)\alpha(-\log\pi(a|s)-\bar{\mathcal H})α(−logπ(a∣s)−Hˉ) to hold the policy entropy near a target Hˉ\bar{\mathcal H}Hˉ, often −dim⁡(A)-\dim(\mathcal A)−dim(A). Together this makes SAC (off-policy, stochastic, twin critics, auto-tuned temperature) the standard sample-efficient method for continuous control, and usually the first thing to try on a new robotics-style task.

Algorithm Policy On/off-policy Action space Key stabilizer Typical use
DQN greedy on Q off discrete replay + target net Atari, small discrete tasks
A2C stochastic on both parallel envs, advantage baseline, simple
PPO stochastic on both clipped ratio, GAE default robust choice; LLM RLHF
DDPG deterministic off continuous target nets, noise historical; brittle
