SAC stochastic (tanh-Gaussian) off continuous entropy bonus, twin critics robotics, sample-efficient control
pythonsac_losses.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, i, o, h=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(i, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, o))
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

class Actor(nn.Module):
    """Tanh-squashed Gaussian policy. Returns an action and its log-probability."""
    def __init__(self, obs_dim, act_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.body = MLP(obs_dim, 2 * act_dim)
    def forward(self, s):
        mu, log_std = self.body(s).chunk(2, dim=-1)
        log_std = log_std.clamp(-5, 2)
        dist = torch.distributions.Normal(mu, log_std.exp())
        u = dist.rsample()                                   # reparameterized sample, keeps gradient
        a = torch.tanh(u)
        # change-of-variables correction for the tanh squashing
        logp = dist.log_prob(u).sum(-1) - (2 * (torch.log(torch.tensor(2.0)) - u - F.softplus(-2 * u))).sum(-1)
        return a, logp

def sac_losses(actor, q1, q2, q1_targ, q2_targ, batch, alpha=0.2, gamma=0.99):
    s, a, r, s2, d = batch                                    # shapes (B,obs) (B,act) (B,) (B,obs) (B,)
    with torch.no_grad():
        a2, logp2 = actor(s2)
        sa2 = torch.cat([s2, a2], -1)
        q_targ = torch.min(q1_targ(sa2), q2_targ(sa2)).squeeze(-1) - alpha * logp2   # soft target
        y = r + gamma * (1 - d) * q_targ
    sa = torch.cat([s, a], -1)
    critic_loss = F.mse_loss(q1(sa).squeeze(-1), y) + F.mse_loss(q2(sa).squeeze(-1), y)
    a_new, logp = actor(s)                                    # fresh actions for the actor loss
    sa_new = torch.cat([s, a_new], -1)
    q_pi = torch.min(q1(sa_new), q2(sa_new)).squeeze(-1)
    actor_loss = (alpha * logp - q_pi).mean()                 # maximize Q + entropy
    return critic_loss, actor_loss

B, od, ad = 32, 8, 2
actor, q1, q2, q1t, q2t = Actor(od, ad), MLP(od + ad, 1), MLP(od + ad, 1), MLP(od + ad, 1), MLP(od + ad, 1)
batch = (torch.randn(B, od), torch.rand(B, ad) * 2 - 1, torch.randn(B), torch.randn(B, od), torch.zeros(B))
cl, al = sac_losses(actor, q1, q2, q1t, q2t, batch)
print(cl.item(), al.item())

In the full algorithm, the critic and actor losses use separate optimizers (the actor loss must not update the critics' parameters, which optimizer.zero_grad() and stepping only the actor's optimizer ensures), and the target critics follow the online critics by Polyak averaging.

Exploration strategies

Exploration is the part of RL with no analogue in supervised learning, and the part where deep RL is still weakest. Strategies form a ladder of increasing sophistication.

  • Undirected noise. ε\varepsilonε-greedy for discrete actions, Gaussian or Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise for continuous ones, and the entropy bonuses of A2C, PPO and SAC. These work when rewards are dense and the task requires only local variations. They fail when reaching any reward requires a long, specific sequence of actions: a random policy has an exponentially small chance of producing it.
  • Optimism in the face of uncertainty. Prefer actions or states whose value is uncertain. UCB for bandits is the template; in deep RL, ensembles of Q-networks (bootstrapped DQN, Osband et al., 2016) provide uncertainty by disagreement and enable deep exploration, where one sampled network's policy is followed for a whole episode (like Thompson sampling).
  • Intrinsic motivation and curiosity. Add a bonus reward for novelty: count-based bonuses β/N(s)\beta/\sqrt{N(s)}β/N(s)​ (extended to high dimensions with pseudo-counts from density models, Bellemare et al., 2016), or prediction-error bonuses. In the Intrinsic Curiosity Module (Pathak et al., 2017) the bonus is the error of a learnt forward model in a learnt feature space; in Random Network Distillation (Burda et al., 2019) it is the error of a predictor network trying to match a fixed random network's output on the state, which is high for states rarely visited. RND was the first method to exceed average human performance on the notoriously hard-exploration Atari game Montezuma's Revenge without demonstrations. A caveat is the noisy TV problem: a purely random source of observations never becomes predictable, and a prediction-error agent can be trapped watching it.
  • Goal-conditioned and structured exploration. Learn skills or subgoals, or maintain an archive of promising states and return to them (Go-Explore, Ecoffet et al., 2019, 2021).
  • Using demonstrations or a pretrained model. Imitation learning gives the agent a good starting distribution. This is the most reliable approach in practice, and in LLM post-training it is the first stage: supervised fine-tuning on human-written examples before any reinforcement learning (see below).
Practical exploration advice

Start with the simplest thing the algorithm provides (entropy bonus for PPO, a decaying ε\varepsilonε for DQN, auto-tuned temperature for SAC), shape the reward only if you must (and then check the agent is not exploiting the shaping), and look at behaviour, not just the return curve. A flat curve at zero return over many episodes is an exploration problem; a curve that rises and collapses is usually an optimization or stability problem.

Model-based RL and world models

Everything so far is model-free: the agent never builds an explicit predictor of what happens next, and it pays for that with sample complexity (DQN needs on the order of 10710^7107 frames per game). Model-based RL learns a model p^(s′∣s,a)\hat p(s'\mid s,a)p^​(s′∣s,a) and r^(s,a)\hat r(s,a)r^(s,a) from experience and then uses it to improve the policy with little or no further environment interaction. Having a model offers two routes.

Planning at decision time. Use the model to search for good actions from the current state. Model predictive control (MPC) samples candidate action sequences, rolls them out in the model for a short horizon, and executes the first action of the best sequence, then replans. PETS (Chua et al., 2018) pairs this with an ensemble of probabilistic neural-network dynamics models so that the planner knows where the model is uncertain. AlphaZero (Silver et al., 2017/2018) plans with Monte Carlo tree search using the known rules of Go, chess and shogi, guided by a policy-value network trained on the search's own outputs; MuZero (Schrittwieser et al., 2020) removes the need for known rules by learning a latent model that predicts only quantities useful for planning (reward, value and policy), and matched AlphaZero in board games while also working on Atari.

Learning from imagined data. Use the model as a simulator to generate extra training experience for a model-free learner. Sutton's Dyna (1990) does this in the tabular case: after each real step, apply the Q-learning update to a few simulated transitions from the model as well. In the deep setting, MBPO (Janner et al., 2019) trains a SAC agent on short model rollouts branched from real states, since long rollouts compound model error.

World models. Ha and Schmidhuber's World Models (2018) trained a VAE to compress frames into latent codes, an RNN to predict the next latent, and a tiny controller acting on the latents, then even trained the controller entirely inside the learnt dream. The Dreamer family (Hafner et al., 2020 onward) learns a recurrent latent dynamics model (the RSSM) from pixels and trains an actor-critic purely on imagined latent trajectories, and later versions solve a wide range of tasks with one set of hyper-parameters. Conceptually, this is the link to generative modelling in Weeks 12 and 13: a world model is a conditional generative model of the future.

The fundamental difficulty is model bias and compounding error. A one-step model with 1% error leads to rollouts that, after 50 steps, drift into regions of state space the model never saw, and the policy optimizer is an adversary that will find and exploit every flaw (just like the actor exploiting an approximate critic). Common remedies are short rollouts, ensembles with uncertainty penalties, and learning the model in a latent space that keeps only decision-relevant information. Model-based methods typically win by an order of magnitude in sample efficiency on continuous control, and the gap narrows when the dynamics are complex or discontinuous (contact-rich manipulation).

Offline reinforcement learning

Offline (batch) RL learns a policy from a fixed dataset of transitions collected by some other behaviour policy, with no environment interaction during training. It matters when exploration is expensive or dangerous (healthcare, autonomous driving, industrial control), and it promises to bring to RL the data-scaling recipe that works in supervised learning. It is also much harder than it looks.

The core problem is distribution shift (Levine, Kumar, Tucker and Fu, 2020, tutorial). An off-policy algorithm such as DQN or SAC queries q(s′,a′)q(s',a')q(s′,a′) at actions a′a'a′ chosen by the learnt policy, including actions that never appear in the dataset. There the Q-function has no data to constrain it, and function approximators extrapolate arbitrarily; the max⁡\maxmax or the actor then seeks out precisely the actions with the highest erroneous values. In online RL the agent tries the action and finds out it was bad. Offline, no correction ever arrives and errors compound through bootstrapping. Naively running DQN or SAC on a fixed dataset typically fails even when the dataset contains expert data.

Offline methods therefore keep the learnt policy close to the data, or keep values pessimistic away from it:

  • Policy constraints (BCQ, Fujimoto et al., 2019; BEAR, Kumar et al., 2019; TD3+BC, Fujimoto and Gu, 2021): restrict or regularize the policy toward the behaviour policy. TD3+BC literally adds a behaviour-cloning term to the TD3 actor loss.
  • Conservative value learning (CQL, Kumar et al., 2020): add a penalty that pushes down Q-values on out-of-distribution actions while keeping them up on dataset actions, so the learnt Q lower-bounds the true value.
  • In-sample methods (IQL, Kostrikov et al., 2022): learn values using only actions that appear in the dataset, via expectile regression, and extract a policy by advantage-weighted regression, never querying unseen actions.
  • Sequence-modelling view (Decision Transformer, Chen et al., 2021): treat trajectories as token sequences of (return-to-go, state, action) and train a causal Transformer by supervised learning to predict actions conditioned on the desired return. It avoids bootstrapping altogether, which makes it simple and stable, at the price of limited ability to stitch together good sub-trajectories from different episodes.
Offline evaluation is hard

You cannot measure a policy's return without running it. Off-policy evaluation with importance sampling has enormous variance over long horizons, and fitted-Q evaluation inherits the extrapolation issue. Many papers therefore report online returns in a simulator, which is not available in the settings that motivate offline RL. Treat reported offline-RL benchmark numbers with care, and when possible keep a small online evaluation budget.

Reinforcement learning and language models

The most consequential application of deep RL today is not a game or a robot but post-training of large language models (Week 10). A pretrained LM is trained to imitate text, which is not the same as being helpful, honest or harmless, or being correct. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) steers the model with a learnt reward signal instead.

Casting text generation as an MDP

Treat the LM as the policy πθ(yt∣x,y<t)\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})πθ​(yt​∣x,y<t​). The state is the prompt xxx plus the tokens generated so far, the action is the next token (a discrete action space of 30k to 200k tokens), and the transition is deterministic (append the token). An episode is one full response y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_1,\dots,y_T)y=(y1​,…,yT​) ending at an end-of-sequence token. Reward is typically given only at the end of the response (a sparse, delayed reward, so credit assignment across hundreds of tokens is the main difficulty) from a reward model, though some implementations add a per-token KL penalty.

Stage 1: supervised fine-tuning

Fine-tune the pretrained model by ordinary cross-entropy on a set of high-quality prompt-response demonstrations written by humans. This gives the RL stage a sensible starting policy (so the early samples are not gibberish) and is the "demonstrations for exploration" idea above. Call the result πref\pi_{\text{ref}}πref​ (the reference or SFT policy).

Stage 2: the reward model

Writing a numeric reward function for "a good answer" is impossible, but people can compare two answers reliably. Collect prompts xxx with pairs of responses (yw,yl)(y_w,y_l)(yw​,yl​), where ywy_wyw​ was preferred. Train a reward model rϕ(x,y)r_{\boldsymbol\phi}(x,y)rϕ​(x,y) (usually the same LM with a scalar head replacing the vocabulary head) under the Bradley-Terry model of preferences, which says the probability that ywy_wyw​ beats yly_lyl​ is a logistic function of the reward difference: P(yw≻yl∣x)=σ(rϕ(x,yw)−rϕ(x,yl)),LRM(ϕ)=−E(x,yw,yl)[log⁡σ(rϕ(x,yw)−rϕ(x,yl))].P(y_w\succ y_l\mid x)=\sigma\big(r_{\boldsymbol\phi}(x,y_w)-r_{\boldsymbol\phi}(x,y_l)\big),\qquad \mathcal L_{\text{RM}}(\boldsymbol\phi)=-\E_{(x,y_w,y_l)}\Big[\log\sigma\big(r_{\boldsymbol\phi}(x,y_w)-r_{\boldsymbol\phi}(x,y_l)\big)\Big].P(yw​≻yl​∣x)=σ(rϕ​(x,yw​)−rϕ​(x,yl​)),LRM​(ϕ)=−E(x,yw​,yl​)​[logσ(rϕ​(x,yw​)−rϕ​(x,yl​))]. This is binary logistic regression on score differences. Only differences matter, so the reward's offset is arbitrary; implementations often normalize rewards. The reward model is a proxy: it is trained on finite human data and is accurate only near the distribution on which it was trained.

Stage 3: policy optimization with a KL penalty

Now optimize the policy against the proxy reward, but anchored to the reference model: max⁡θ  Ex∼D, y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[rϕ(x,y)]−β Ex[DKL(πθ(⋅∣x) ∥ πref(⋅∣x))].\max_{\boldsymbol\theta}\;\E_{x\sim\mathcal D,\ y\sim\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\Big[r_{\boldsymbol\phi}(x,y)\Big]-\beta\,\E_x\Big[\KL\big(\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\Big].θmax​Ex∼D, y∼πθ​(⋅∣x)​[rϕ​(x,y)]−βEx​[DKL​(πθ​(⋅∣x)∥πref​(⋅∣x))]. The KL term does the work that the trust region does in PPO, but over the whole training run. It keeps the policy where the reward model is reliable, prevents mode collapse onto a single high-reward string, and preserves fluency. Without it, the policy finds inputs on which the reward model gives high scores for the wrong reasons: reward hacking, a form of Goodhart's law. Gao, Schulman and Hilton (2023) measured this "overoptimization" with a synthetic gold reward model and found that the gold reward first rises and then falls as the policy moves further (in KL) from the initial policy while the proxy reward keeps rising. The optimization is run with PPO: the value function is a second network (often initialized from the reward model), advantages come from GAE over tokens with the per-token KL penalty included in the reward, and the clipped objective keeps each batch update small. That makes RLHF with PPO resource-heavy: you hold in memory the policy, the reference model, the reward model and the value model.

pythonrlhf_reward_loss.py
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def reward_model_loss(r_chosen, r_rejected):
    """Bradley-Terry loss. Both tensors have shape (B,): scalar rewards for preferred / dispreferred responses."""
    return -F.logsigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected).mean()

def kl_shaped_token_rewards(logp_policy, logp_ref, final_reward, beta=0.05):
    """Per-token rewards for PPO in RLHF. logp_* have shape (B, T) (log-prob of each sampled token under the
    policy / reference); final_reward (B,) is the reward-model score given to the last token only.
    Per-token reward = -beta * (logp_policy - logp_ref), plus the sequence reward at the final position."""
    rewards = -beta * (logp_policy - logp_ref)             # sampled estimate of the KL penalty, per token
    rewards[:, -1] = rewards[:, -1] + final_reward
    return rewards

B, T = 4, 6
print(reward_model_loss(torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 3.0]), torch.tensor([1.0, 1.5, -0.5, 0.0])).item())
print(kl_shaped_token_rewards(torch.randn(B, T) - 2, torch.randn(B, T) - 2, torch.randn(B)).shape)

DPO: the same objective without an explicit RL loop

The KL-regularized objective above has a closed-form optimal policy, π∗(y∣x)∝πref(y∣x)exp⁡(r(x,y)/β)\pi^*(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\big(r(x,y)/\beta\big)π∗(y∣x)∝πref​(y∣x)exp(r(x,y)/β). Rearranging gives the reward as r(x,y)=βlog⁡π∗(y∣x)πref(y∣x)+βlog⁡Z(x)r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi^*(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}+\beta\log Z(x)r(x,y)=βlogπref​(y∣x)π∗(y∣x)​+βlogZ(x), where the partition function Z(x)Z(x)Z(x) cancels when two responses to the same prompt are compared in the Bradley-Terry model. Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) substitutes this implicit reward into the preference loss and obtains a supervised objective on the policy itself: LDPO(θ)=−E(x,yw,yl)[log⁡σ(βlog⁡πθ(yw∣x)πref(yw∣x)−βlog⁡πθ(yl∣x)πref(yl∣x))].\mathcal L_{\text{DPO}}(\boldsymbol\theta)=-\E_{(x,y_w,y_l)}\Big[\log\sigma\Big(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\Big)\Big].LDPO​(θ)=−E(x,yw​,yl​)​[logσ(βlogπref​(yw​∣x)πθ​(yw​∣x)​−βlogπref​(yl​∣x)πθ​(yl​∣x)​)]. There is no reward model to train, no sampling from the policy during training, and no value function: just a classification-style loss on fixed preference pairs, needing the log-probabilities of both responses under the current and reference models. It optimizes the same KL-regularized objective, assuming the Bradley-Terry model. The trade-offs: DPO is simpler, cheaper and more stable; but it is offline with respect to the preference data (it never explores beyond the responses in the dataset, so it can suffer the distribution-shift issues of the offline section), and online RL with a reward model can exploit fresh samples and, when a verifiable reward exists, optimize it directly. Which approach wins depends on the data and task and is an active empirical question, so treat claims of one dominating the other with care.

GRPO and verifiable rewards

For tasks where correctness can be checked automatically, such as math answers or code that passes unit tests, a learnt reward model is unnecessary: use the checker as the reward ("reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards"). Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper (Shao et al., 2024) and used for DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025), keeps PPO's clipped objective and KL penalty but drops the learnt value function. For each prompt it samples a group of GGG responses, scores them, and uses the group's own statistics as the baseline: A^i=Ri−mean⁡(R1,…,RG)std⁡(R1,…,RG).\hat A_i=\frac{R_i-\operatorname{mean}(R_1,\dots,R_G)}{\operatorname{std}(R_1,\dots,R_G)}.A^i​=std(R1​,…,RG​)Ri​−mean(R1​,…,RG​)​. Every token in response iii shares the advantage A^i\hat A_iA^i​. This is the baseline trick again, with the baseline estimated by Monte Carlo from sibling samples instead of a critic, which saves the memory and compute of the value network and avoids having to train a good critic over long sequences. It is closely related to the leave-one-out baselines used in REINFORCE-style RLHF (e.g. RLOO, Ahmadian et al., 2024). The price is that the group must be large enough for the baseline to be informative, and prompts for which all samples are right or all wrong provide no gradient.

What is and is not settled

The following are well established: RLHF with PPO and a KL penalty works for instruction following; reward models are imperfect proxies that can be over-optimized; DPO and GRPO are simplified relatives that share PPO's ideas (preference or group-relative signals, KL anchoring to a reference). Less settled: how much of the reasoning ability gained by RL with verifiable rewards is new capability versus better elicitation of what pretraining already provided, and which of PPO, DPO, GRPO and their variants is best in a given setting. Expect this part of the field to change quickly.

Lab: DQN on CartPole, then PPO with Stable-Baselines3

In this lab you build a complete DQN from scratch in PyTorch (about 100 lines), train it on Gymnasium's CartPole-v1, then solve the same task with PPO from the Stable-Baselines3 library and compare. In CartPole the state is four numbers (cart position, cart velocity, pole angle, pole angular velocity), there are two actions (push left or right), the reward is +1 per step, and an episode ends when the pole tilts more than about 12 degrees, the cart leaves the track, or after 500 steps. Return 500 is a perfect score. Install with pip install torch gymnasium stable-baselines3 (Colab has most of this).

Step 1: the replay buffer and Q-network

pythondqn_cartpole.py
import random
from collections import deque
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import gymnasium as gym

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

class ReplayBuffer:
    """Fixed-size FIFO buffer of (s, a, r, s', terminated) transitions with uniform sampling."""
    def __init__(self, capacity, obs_dim):
        self.cap, self.i, self.n = capacity, 0, 0
        self.s = np.zeros((capacity, obs_dim), dtype=np.float32)
        self.s2 = np.zeros((capacity, obs_dim), dtype=np.float32)
        self.a = np.zeros(capacity, dtype=np.int64)
        self.r = np.zeros(capacity, dtype=np.float32)
        self.d = np.zeros(capacity, dtype=np.float32)

    def add(self, s, a, r, s2, d):
        self.s[self.i], self.a[self.i], self.r[self.i], self.s2[self.i], self.d[self.i] = s, a, r, s2, d
        self.i = (self.i + 1) % self.cap
        self.n = min(self.n + 1, self.cap)

    def sample(self, batch_size):
        idx = np.random.randint(0, self.n, size=batch_size)
        t = lambda x: torch.as_tensor(x[idx], device=device)
        return t(self.s), t(self.a), t(self.r), t(self.s2), t(self.d)

class QNet(nn.Module):
    """MLP that maps an observation (B, 4) to one Q-value per action (B, 2)."""
    def __init__(self, obs_dim, n_actions, hidden=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(obs_dim, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, n_actions),
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

Step 2: the training loop

Note the two details that most often go wrong: the done flag used for bootstrapping must be terminated (a true terminal state), not truncated (time limit), and targets are computed without gradient.

pythondqn_train.py
def train_dqn(total_steps=30_000, gamma=0.99, lr=1e-3, batch_size=64, buffer_size=50_000,
              learning_starts=1_000, train_freq=1, target_tau=0.01, eps_start=1.0, eps_end=0.05,
              eps_decay_steps=10_000, double=True, seed=0, verbose=True):
    env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
    obs_dim, n_actions = env.observation_space.shape[0], env.action_space.n
    random.seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
    online, target = QNet(obs_dim, n_actions).to(device), QNet(obs_dim, n_actions).to(device)
    target.load_state_dict(online.state_dict())
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(online.parameters(), lr=lr)
    buf = ReplayBuffer(buffer_size, obs_dim)

    s, _ = env.reset(seed=seed)
    ep_return, returns = 0.0, []
    for step in range(1, total_steps + 1):
        eps = max(eps_end, eps_start - (eps_start - eps_end) * step / eps_decay_steps)
        if random.random() < eps:
            a = env.action_space.sample()
        else:
            with torch.no_grad():
                a = int(online(torch.as_tensor(s, device=device).unsqueeze(0)).argmax(dim=1).item())
        s2, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(a)
        buf.add(s, a, r, s2, float(terminated))          # bootstrap through truncation, not termination
        s, ep_return = s2, ep_return + r
        if terminated or truncated:
            returns.append(ep_return)
            s, _ = env.reset()
            ep_return = 0.0

        if step >= learning_starts and step % train_freq == 0:
            bs, ba, br, bs2, bd = buf.sample(batch_size)
            with torch.no_grad():
                if double:                                # Double DQN: online selects, target evaluates
                    a_star = online(bs2).argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True)
                    q_next = target(bs2).gather(1, a_star).squeeze(1)
                else:
                    q_next = target(bs2).max(dim=1).values
                y = br + gamma * (1.0 - bd) * q_next
            q = online(bs).gather(1, ba.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)    # Q(s, a_taken), shape (B,)
            loss = F.smooth_l1_loss(q, y)                 # Huber loss
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(online.parameters(), 10.0)
            opt.step()
            with torch.no_grad():                         # Polyak (soft) target update
                for p_t, p in zip(target.parameters(), online.parameters()):
                    p_t.mul_(1 - target_tau).add_(target_tau * p)

        if verbose and step % 2_000 == 0 and returns:
            print(f"step {step:6d} | eps {eps:.2f} | mean return (last 10) {np.mean(returns[-10:]):6.1f} | loss {loss.item() if step >= learning_starts else float('nan'):.4f}")
    return online, returns

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model, returns = train_dqn()

On a typical run, the mean return climbs from about 20 (random behaviour) to several hundred within 20,000 to 30,000 steps, though DQN on CartPole is noisy and often oscillates (it may reach 500, collapse, and recover). Different seeds will differ a lot, so run at least three and plot the mean. This variability is a typical feature of deep RL, not a bug in your code.

Step 3: evaluate the greedy policy and inspect Q-values

pythondqn_eval.py
def evaluate(model, episodes=10, seed=100):
    env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
    scores = []
    for k in range(episodes):
        s, _ = env.reset(seed=seed + k)
        done, total = False, 0.0
        while not done:
            with torch.no_grad():
                a = int(model(torch.as_tensor(s, device=device).unsqueeze(0)).argmax(dim=1).item())
            s, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(a)
            total += r
            done = terminated or truncated
        scores.append(total)
    return np.mean(scores), np.std(scores)

mean, std = evaluate(model)
print(f"greedy evaluation: {mean:.1f} +- {std:.1f}")
# Sanity check on the value scale: with r = +1 per step and gamma = 0.99, the maximum possible
# discounted return is (1 - 0.99**500)/(1 - 0.99) ~= 99.3, so Q(s, a) should never exceed about 100.
s0, _ = gym.make("CartPole-v1").reset(seed=0)
print("Q(s0, .) =", model(torch.as_tensor(s0, device=device).unsqueeze(0)).detach().cpu().numpy())

The last lines show a useful debugging habit: compute the maximum possible value analytically and check that your learnt Q-values respect it. If they greatly exceed it, you have an overestimation or target bug.

Step 4: PPO with Stable-Baselines3

pythonppo_sb3.py
import gymnasium as gym
from stable_baselines3 import PPO
from stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env
from stable_baselines3.common.evaluation import evaluate_policy

# 8 parallel environments, as in A2C/PPO: the batch diversity replaces the replay buffer
vec_env = make_vec_env("CartPole-v1", n_envs=8, seed=0)

model = PPO(
    "MlpPolicy", vec_env,
    n_steps=256,            # rollout length per env -> batch of 8 * 256 = 2048 samples per update
    batch_size=64,          # minibatch size for the SGD epochs
    n_epochs=10,            # K epochs per batch
    gamma=0.99, gae_lambda=0.95,
    clip_range=0.2,
    ent_coef=0.0, vf_coef=0.5,
    learning_rate=3e-4,
    verbose=1, seed=0,
)
model.learn(total_timesteps=100_000)

eval_env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
mean_r, std_r = evaluate_policy(model, eval_env, n_eval_episodes=20, deterministic=True)
print(f"PPO evaluation: {mean_r:.1f} +- {std_r:.1f}")
model.save("ppo_cartpole")

With verbose=1, SB3 prints a table at every update including approx_kl, clip_fraction, entropy_loss, explained_variance and value_loss. Learn to read these: explained_variance near 1 means the critic predicts returns well, clip_fraction shows what share of samples hit the clip, and approx_kl should stay small (about 0.01 or lower).

Step 5: experiments to run

  1. Ablate the stabilizers. Set target_tau=1.0 (target network equals online network), then set buffer_size to 64 (almost no replay) and compare learning curves over three seeds each. Which stabilizer matters more on CartPole?
  2. Double vs vanilla. Run double=False versus double=True and print the mean predicted Q-value at the start state. Vanilla values tend to be higher.
  3. PPO hyper-parameters. Vary clip_range in {0.05, 0.2, 0.5} and n_epochs in {3, 10, 30}, tracking approx_kl and the final return.
  4. Sample efficiency. Plot return against environment steps for DQN and PPO. On CartPole both solve the task; which needs fewer environment steps in your runs, and what changes if you count wall-clock time?
  5. Discount. Try γ∈{0.9,0.99,0.999}\gamma\in\{0.9,0.99,0.999\}γ∈{0.9,0.99,0.999} for DQN. A short horizon makes the task look easier but can fail to look far enough ahead.

Common mistakes and debugging tips

Deep RL bugs are especially hard because the failure symptom ("the return does not go up") fits dozens of causes, and the training signal is noisy. Check cheap, deterministic things first.

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Q-values explode or grow without bound Missing target network, or targets not detached; learning rate too high; no reward scaling Use torch.no_grad() for targets, soft target updates, Huber loss, gradient clipping, smaller LR
Q-values far above the maximum possible return Overestimation (max over noisy values), or bootstrapping through terminal states Double DQN or twin critics; multiply bootstrap by (1 - terminated)
Agent learns nothing; return flat at the random level Exploration too weak, reward never seen, or learning never started (learning_starts larger than steps) Check the minimum number of steps to reach a reward, raise entropy bonus or epsilon, verify the buffer is filling
Return rises then collapses (policy gradient) Updates too large, no advantage normalization, learning rate too high Smaller LR, lower clip range, fewer epochs, watch approx_kl; early-stop an update when KL is large
Value loss large and critic fails to fit Returns on very different scales Normalize observations and rewards (running statistics), use value clipping or a Huber loss
Time-limit episodes treated as failures Using done = terminated or truncated in the bootstrap Bootstrap through truncation: use only terminated for the (1 - done) mask
Policy collapses to deterministic too early Entropy too low, or log_std initialized small Entropy bonus, larger initial std, SAC auto-temperature
Works for one seed, not for the next High variance of RL Run 5 to 10 seeds, report mean and a confidence interval, never a best-of-seeds curve
Off-by-one in returns or GAE Ordering errors in backward recursions; forgetting to cut at episode ends Unit-test GAE on a hand-computed 3-step example; test with a constant-reward environment where the answer is known
Training uses stale data in an on-policy method Reusing an old batch or an old log-prob Recompute old_logp at collection time; discard the batch after KKK epochs
A debugging order that saves days
  1. Test your algorithm on a trivial environment where you know the answer (a one-step bandit, or a 2-state chain). It must solve it in seconds.
  2. Check the data: print a few (s, a, r, s', done) tuples and confirm shapes, dtypes, and that rewards are what you expect.
  3. Check a scale: what are the largest plausible returns and Q-values? Do the network's outputs obey it?
  4. Log diagnostics every update: episode return and length, loss terms, policy entropy, approximate KL, clip fraction, explained variance, gradient norm, mean ∣Q∣|Q|∣Q∣.
  5. Only then tune hyper-parameters, one at a time, with several seeds. "Deep reinforcement learning that matters" (Henderson et al., 2018) documents how easy it is to draw wrong conclusions from too few seeds.

Exercise 1: Bellman by hand

A deterministic chain has states s1→s2→terminals_1\to s_2\to\text{terminal}s1​→s2​→terminal under the only available policy, with rewards R=1R=1R=1 for leaving s1s_1s1​ and R=2R=2R=2 for leaving s2s_2s2​. With γ=0.5\gamma=0.5γ=0.5, compute vπ(s1)v_\pi(s_1)vπ​(s1​) and vπ(s2)v_\pi(s_2)vπ​(s2​) (a) from the definition of the return, and (b) by solving the Bellman expectation equations. Then state what changes at γ=1\gamma=1γ=1 and why this is still well defined.

Solution

(a) From s2s_2s2​: G=2G=2G=2, so v(s2)=2v(s_2)=2v(s2​)=2. From s1s_1s1​: G=1+γ⋅2=1+0.5⋅2=2G=1+\gamma\cdot2=1+0.5\cdot2=2G=1+γ⋅2=1+0.5⋅2=2, so v(s1)=2v(s_1)=2v(s1​)=2. (b) The equations are v(s2)=2+γ⋅0v(s_2)=2+\gamma\cdot0v(s2​)=2+γ⋅0 (terminal value is zero) and v(s1)=1+γv(s2)v(s_1)=1+\gamma v(s_2)v(s1​)=1+γv(s2​), which give the same numbers. At γ=1\gamma=1γ=1: v(s2)=2v(s_2)=2v(s2​)=2, v(s1)=3v(s_1)=3v(s1​)=3; the sum is finite because the episode has finite length, so the undiscounted return is well defined.

Exercise 2: Q-learning versus SARSA update

In state s′s's′ the current estimates are Q(s′,a1)=2Q(s',a_1)=2Q(s′,a1​)=2 and Q(s′,a2)=1Q(s',a_2)=1Q(s′,a2​)=1. You have Q(s,a)=0.5Q(s,a)=0.5Q(s,a)=0.5, observe r=1r=1r=1, move to s′s's′, and the ε\varepsilonε-greedy behaviour policy happens to choose the exploratory action a2a_2a2​ there. With α=0.1\alpha=0.1α=0.1 and γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9, compute the updated Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) under SARSA and under Q-learning. Which one would be unchanged if the behaviour policy had picked a1a_1a1​?

Solution

Q-learning target: 1+0.9max⁡(2,1)=2.81+0.9\max(2,1)=2.81+0.9max(2,1)=2.8, so Q←0.5+0.1(2.8−0.5)=0.73Q\leftarrow0.5+0.1(2.8-0.5)=0.73Q←0.5+0.1(2.8−0.5)=0.73. SARSA target uses the action actually chosen, a2a_2a2​: 1+0.9⋅1=1.91+0.9\cdot1=1.91+0.9⋅1=1.9, so Q←0.5+0.1(1.9−0.5)=0.64Q\leftarrow0.5+0.1(1.9-0.5)=0.64Q←0.5+0.1(1.9−0.5)=0.64. If a1a_1a1​ had been picked, both targets equal 2.82.82.8 and the two updates agree (0.73). Q-learning's target never depends on the exploratory choice, which is exactly what "off-policy" means here.

Exercise 5: Why the baseline is unbiased

Show that Ea∼πθ(⋅∣s)[∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s) b(s)]=0\E_{a\sim\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\cdot|s)}\big[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\log\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}(a\mid s)\,b(s)\big]=\mathbf 0Ea∼πθ​(⋅∣s)​[∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)b(s)]=0 for any function bbb of the state. Then, for a one-dimensional Gaussian policy π(a∣s)=N(μθ(s),σ2)\pi(a|s)=\mathcal N(\mu_{\boldsymbol\theta}(s),\sigma^2)π(a∣s)=N(μθ​(s),σ2) with fixed σ\sigmaσ, compute ∇μlog⁡π(a∣s)\nabla_\mu\log\pi(a|s)∇μ​logπ(a∣s) and explain in words what the policy-gradient update does to μ\muμ when the advantage is positive.

Solution

For discrete actions, ∑aπ(a∣s)∇log⁡π(a∣s) b(s)=b(s)∑a∇π(a∣s)=b(s)∇∑aπ(a∣s)=b(s)∇1=0\sum_a\pi(a|s)\nabla\log\pi(a|s)\,b(s)=b(s)\sum_a\nabla\pi(a|s)=b(s)\nabla\sum_a\pi(a|s)=b(s)\nabla1=0∑a​π(a∣s)∇logπ(a∣s)b(s)=b(s)∑a​∇π(a∣s)=b(s)∇∑a​π(a∣s)=b(s)∇1=0; for continuous actions replace the sum by an integral (interchanging gradient and integral under standard regularity). For the Gaussian, log⁡π=−(a−μ)22σ2+const\log\pi=-\frac{(a-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}+\text{const}logπ=−2σ2(a−μ)2​+const, so ∇μlog⁡π=(a−μ)/σ2\nabla_\mu\log\pi=(a-\mu)/\sigma^2∇μ​logπ=(a−μ)/σ2. With positive advantage, the update moves μ\muμ toward the sampled action aaa (the step is proportional to (a−μ)/σ2⋅A(a-\mu)/\sigma^2\cdot A(a−μ)/σ2⋅A); with negative advantage it moves μ\muμ away from it. Note the 1/σ21/\sigma^21/σ2 factor: smaller σ\sigmaσ gives larger, noisier updates to the mean.

Exercise 6: A dueling head

Write a PyTorch nn.Module for a dueling Q-network for an input of dimension obs_dim and n_actions actions, with a shared 128-unit hidden layer and separate value and advantage heads, using the mean-advantage subtraction. Check that adding a constant to the advantage head's output leaves QQQ unchanged.

Solution
python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class DuelingQNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, obs_dim, n_actions, hidden=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.trunk = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(obs_dim, hidden), nn.ReLU())
        self.value = nn.Linear(hidden, 1)              # V(s): (B, 1)
        self.adv = nn.Linear(hidden, n_actions)        # A(s, a): (B, n_actions)

    def forward(self, x, adv_shift=0.0):
        h = self.trunk(x)
        v, a = self.value(h), self.adv(h) + adv_shift   # adv_shift only used for the invariance check
        return v + a - a.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True)      # (B, n_actions)

net = DuelingQNet(4, 2)
x = torch.randn(5, 4)
print(torch.allclose(net(x), net(x, adv_shift=3.7), atol=1e-6))   # True: shift cancels in the mean

The identifiability problem is resolved because only advantages relative to their mean affect QQQ.

Exercise 7: Overestimation by the max

Let X1,X2X_1,X_2X1​,X2​ be independent N(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1)N(0,1) estimates of two actions whose true values are both 0. Compute E[max⁡(X1,X2)]\E[\max(X_1,X_2)]E[max(X1​,X2​)] exactly. Then explain why selecting with X1,X2X_1,X_2X1​,X2​ and evaluating with an independent second pair Y1,Y2Y_1,Y_2Y1​,Y2​ removes the bias.

Solution

max⁡(X1,X2)=12(X1+X2)+12∣X1−X2∣\max(X_1,X_2)=\tfrac12(X_1+X_2)+\tfrac12|X_1-X_2|max(X1​,X2​)=21​(X1​+X2​)+21​∣X1​−X2​∣. The first term has mean 0. X1−X2∼N(0,2)X_1-X_2\sim\mathcal N(0,2)X1​−X2​∼N(0,2), so E∣X1−X2∣=2⋅2/π=2/π\E|X_1-X_2|=\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt{2/\pi}=2/\sqrt\piE∣X1​−X2​∣=2​⋅2/π​=2/π​. Hence E[max⁡]=12⋅2/π=1/π≈0.564\E[\max]=\tfrac12\cdot2/\sqrt\pi=1/\sqrt\pi\approx0.564E[max]=21​⋅2/π​=1/π​≈0.564, matching the chart (0.56). In the double estimator the action a^=arg max⁡iXi\hat a=\argmax_iX_ia^=argmaxi​Xi​ is chosen by XXX, but evaluated with Ya^Y_{\hat a}Ya^​, which is independent of the selection event and has mean 0, so E[Ya^]=0\E[Y_{\hat a}]=0E[Ya^​]=0: the evaluation noise no longer correlates with the selection noise.

Exercise 8 (challenging): A divergent off-policy TD example

Consider two states with a linear value function V(s1)=wV(s_1)=wV(s1​)=w, V(s2)=2wV(s_2)=2wV(s2​)=2w (a single weight, features 1 and 2). All rewards are 0. The only transition is s1→s2s_1\to s_2s1​→s2​, and s2s_2s2​ transitions to itself (continuing task). Training updates only on transitions out of s1s_1s1​ (off-policy: the data distribution never samples s2s_2s2​) using semi-gradient TD(0) with step size α\alphaα and discount γ\gammaγ. Derive the update of www, find the condition on γ\gammaγ under which www diverges from any non-zero start, and relate it to the deadly triad. What happens if we also train on transitions out of s2s_2s2​ with the on-policy frequency?

Solution

The TD error at s1s_1s1​ is δ=0+γV(s2)−V(s1)=2γw−w=(2γ−1)w\delta=0+\gamma V(s_2)-V(s_1)=2\gamma w-w=(2\gamma-1)wδ=0+γV(s2​)−V(s1​)=2γw−w=(2γ−1)w, and ∇wV(s1)=1\nabla_wV(s_1)=1∇w​V(s1​)=1. So w←w+α(2γ−1)w=(1+α(2γ−1))ww\leftarrow w+\alpha(2\gamma-1)w=\big(1+\alpha(2\gamma-1)\big)ww←w+α(2γ−1)w=(1+α(2γ−1))w. For γ>1/2\gamma>1/2γ>1/2 the factor exceeds 1 and ∣w∣→∞|w|\to\infty∣w∣→∞ geometrically, even though the true values are all zero (w=0w=0w=0 is the fixed point). All three triad ingredients are present: linear function approximation (shared weight), bootstrapping (target uses V(s2)V(s_2)V(s2​)), off-policy sampling (only s1s_1s1​ updates). On-policy, the stationary distribution of this chain puts all its mass on the absorbing state s2s_2s2​, so the updates come from s2s_2s2​: the TD error there is 2γw−2w=2(γ−1)w2\gamma w-2w=2(\gamma-1)w2γw−2w=2(γ−1)w with gradient 2, giving w←(1−4α(1−γ))ww\leftarrow\big(1-4\alpha(1-\gamma)\big)ww←(1−4α(1−γ))w, which converges to 0 for small α\alphaα. Mixing the two kinds of updates at weights d1,d2d_1,d_2d1​,d2​ gives a net factor 1+α(d1(2γ−1)−4d2(1−γ))1+\alpha\big(d_1(2\gamma-1)-4d_2(1-\gamma)\big)1+α(d1​(2γ−1)−4d2​(1−γ)), so divergence depends on how far the sampling distribution is from the on-policy one. This is the Tsitsiklis and Van Roy style example that Sutton and Barto use to motivate the triad.

Exercise 9 (challenging): Derive DPO

Starting from the KL-regularized objective max⁡πEy∼π[r(x,y)]−βDKL(π∥πref)\max_\pi\E_{y\sim\pi}[r(x,y)]-\beta\KL(\pi\|\pi_{\text{ref}})maxπ​Ey∼π​[r(x,y)]−βDKL​(π∥πref​) for a fixed prompt xxx, (a) show that the optimal policy is π∗(y∣x)=πref(y∣x)exp⁡(r(x,y)/β)/Z(x)\pi^*(y|x)=\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)/Z(x)π∗(y∣x)=πref​(y∣x)exp(r(x,y)/β)/Z(x), (b) express rrr in terms of π∗\pi^*π∗, and (c) substitute into the Bradley-Terry loss to obtain the DPO loss. Why does Z(x)Z(x)Z(x) disappear?

Solution

(a) The objective is ∑yπ(y)[r(y)−βlog⁡π(y)+βlog⁡πref(y)]=−β∑yπ(y)log⁡π(y)πref(y)exp⁡(r(y)/β)\sum_y\pi(y)\big[r(y)-\beta\log\pi(y)+\beta\log\pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\big]=-\beta\sum_y\pi(y)\log\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\exp(r(y)/\beta)}∑y​π(y)[r(y)−βlogπ(y)+βlogπref​(y)]=−β∑y​π(y)logπref​(y)exp(r(y)/β)π(y)​. Let Z=∑yπref(y)exp⁡(r(y)/β)Z=\sum_y\pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\exp(r(y)/\beta)Z=∑y​πref​(y)exp(r(y)/β) and q(y)=πref(y)exp⁡(r(y)/β)/Zq(y)=\pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\exp(r(y)/\beta)/Zq(y)=πref​(y)exp(r(y)/β)/Z, a valid distribution. Then the objective equals −β DKL(π∥q)+βlog⁡Z-\beta\,\KL(\pi\|q)+\beta\log Z−βDKL​(π∥q)+βlogZ, which is maximized (value βlog⁡Z\beta\log ZβlogZ) at π=q\pi=qπ=q. (b) Taking logs, r(y)=βlog⁡π∗(y)πref(y)+βlog⁡Z(x)r(y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi^*(y)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y)}+\beta\log Z(x)r(y)=βlogπref​(y)π∗(y)​+βlogZ(x). (c) The Bradley-Terry probability depends on r(x,yw)−r(x,yl)r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l)r(x,yw​)−r(x,yl​), and βlog⁡Z(x)\beta\log Z(x)βlogZ(x) appears in both, so it cancels: the difference is βlog⁡π∗(yw)πref(yw)−βlog⁡π∗(yl)πref(yl)\beta\log\frac{\pi^*(y_w)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi^*(y_l)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l)}βlogπref​(yw​)π∗(yw​)​−βlogπref​(yl​)π∗(yl​)​. Replacing the unknown π∗\pi^*π∗ by the trainable πθ\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}πθ​ and taking the negative log-likelihood of the observed preferences gives exactly the LDPO\mathcal L_{\text{DPO}}LDPO​ on this page.

Exercise 10: What would happen if...

For each change to the DQN code in the lab, predict the symptom and the reason: (a) remove torch.no_grad() and .detach() so gradients flow into the target; (b) use done = terminated or truncated in the bootstrap mask; (c) set buffer_size=64; (d) set gamma=0.999; (e) in RLHF, set the KL coefficient β\betaβ to 0.

Solution

(a) The loss now also moves the target toward the prediction (a residual gradient); learning is typically slower and biased toward trivially consistent but poor value functions, and it uses extra memory. (b) At time-limit truncations the agent is told the state has value zero though it does not, so values near step 500 are biased low and the agent can learn that "survive long" is worthless; use only terminated. (c) The buffer holds only recent, correlated transitions: the minibatch is nearly one trajectory segment, so learning is unstable and forgets earlier behaviour. (d) The effective horizon is about 1000 steps, longer than any episode; values are large and updates propagate slowly, so learning slows and targets are more sensitive to error. (e) The policy is free to move anywhere that raises the proxy reward: reward hacking, loss of fluency, mode collapse to a few high-scoring outputs, and a falling true quality while the proxy score rises.

Exercise 11 (coding): Tabular Q-learning on the slippery gridworld

Using the transition tensors P and R from the value-iteration code, implement tabular Q-learning with ε\varepsilonε-greedy exploration by sampling transitions from P. Compare the learnt greedy policy and max⁡aQ(s,a)\max_aQ(s,a)maxa​Q(s,a) with the value-iteration solution after 50,000 steps.

Solution
python
import numpy as np

def q_learning(P, R, gamma, goal, pit, steps=50_000, alpha=0.1, eps=0.2, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    nS, nA, _ = P.shape
    Q = np.zeros((nS, nA))
    s = 0
    for _ in range(steps):
        a = rng.integers(nA) if rng.random() < eps else int(np.argmax(Q[s] + 1e-9 * rng.random(nA)))
        s2 = rng.choice(nS, p=P[s, a])                     # sample next state from the model
        target = R[s, a, s2] + (0.0 if s2 in (goal, pit) else gamma * Q[s2].max())
        Q[s, a] += alpha * (target - Q[s, a])
        s = 0 if s2 in (goal, pit) else s2                 # restart after a terminal state
    return Q

# Q = q_learning(P, R, gamma, goal, pit)
# print(np.abs(Q.max(1) - V).max())   # should be small (a few hundredths) away from rarely visited states

Expect the values to agree closely on frequently visited states and to be noisier (or still close to zero) in states the exploratory policy rarely reaches, and expect that a constant step size leaves a residual noise floor proportional to α\alphaα.

Key takeaways

Key takeaways
  • An MDP, with the Markov property, a policy, a discount, and value functions vπ,qπv_\pi,q_\pivπ​,qπ​, is the common language. The Bellman equations express a value as immediate reward plus discounted successor value, and the optimality equations replace the policy average by a max.
  • Dynamic programming needs a model; Monte Carlo is unbiased but high-variance; TD bootstraps for low variance at the price of bias. Q-learning is off-policy (learns q∗q_*q∗​), SARSA is on-policy.
  • Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data together (the deadly triad) can diverge. DQN's replay buffer, target network and Huber loss are practical antidotes; Double DQN fixes max-overestimation, Dueling separates VVV and AAA, prioritized replay samples by TD error.
  • The policy gradient theorem ∇J=E[∑t∇log⁡π(at∣st) Gt]\nabla J=\E[\sum_t\nabla\log\pi(a_t|s_t)\,G_t]∇J=E[∑t​∇logπ(at​∣st​)Gt​] needs no model; baselines (best: vπv_\pivπ​) cut variance without bias; actor-critic bootstraps; GAE(γ,λ)(\gamma,\lambda)(γ,λ) =∑l(γλ)lδt+l=\sum_l(\gamma\lambda)^l\delta_{t+l}=∑l​(γλ)lδt+l​ trades bias for variance.
  • PPO's clipped objective approximates TRPO's trust region cheaply and is the default on-policy algorithm; watch KL and clip fraction. SAC and TD3 are the standard off-policy methods for continuous control, SAC adding a maximum-entropy objective.
  • Exploration is the hard part: entropy and ε\varepsilonε for easy tasks, curiosity or count bonuses for sparse ones. Model-based RL buys sample efficiency at the price of model error; offline RL must contend with distribution shift via conservatism or in-sample learning.
  • RLHF = SFT, then a Bradley-Terry reward model, then PPO with a KL anchor to the reference policy. DPO optimizes the same KL-regularized objective with a supervised loss on preference pairs; GRPO drops the critic in favour of group-relative baselines.
  • RL results are noisy: use several seeds, log diagnostics, and test on trivial environments first.
